304. Departmental administration, $1,886,095.
May I ask whether the Postmaster General has a statement to make lefore we go on with the item?

In introducing these estimates, Mr. Chairman, I will attempt to review briefly the operations of my department since the last time the estimates came before this house, explaining some of those aspects of the operations which are not covered in detail in the department's annual report. In making this presentation I cannot help but feel that I enjoy a great advantage which was denied my predecessors in office during the period since 1953, namely that I shall not be obliged to deal with the questions of the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace who had a great deal of curiosity about the department.
I think the minister will find there are others who have curiosity about the department as presently administered.

As
is well known, the Post Office Department is a vast one extending into every part of Canada and serving every Canadian. Less well known is the fact that in terms of staff it is the second largest government department, being exceeded in size only by the Department of National Defence. Some 25,000 civil servants plus another 25,000 people composed of revenue postmasters, rural mail carriers and various other categories, handle an average of 10 million letters a day through 12,000 post offices. Each day our rural mail deliveries cover 133,000 miles; translated into other figures this represents the fantastic annual equivalent of some 55 return trips to the moon. In the cities, letter carriers in the course of their work walk over 6 million miles a year-an equivalent figure is 240 times around the world. An average letter posted in a street letter box in one city and delivered to its destination in another will undergo a minimum of ten individual handlings in the course of its journey; yet the post office is so smoothly functioning and so efficient that the same first class letter deposited in any major city in Canada will normally be delivered within 24 hours in most other major centres in our country.
On the other hand, the department does not claim perfection; human beings are fallible, and in the process of handling these 10 million letters a day to which I have 57071-3-171
Supply-Post Office
referred it is impossible to avoid the occasional mistake. The percentage of error, however, is extremely small, on an average one hundredth of one per cent or one piece of mail in ten thousand, which figure represents delays, mis-sorted mail and even the occasional letter which disappears and can never be found. But compared with any business operation of which I am aware I think the record of the post office is outstanding.
I will now review the financial operations of the department. The year 1956-57, which is covered by the report available to members of the house, showed total revenues of close to $168 million with total expenditures of just over $162 million, and a favourable balance of $5,827,000. I am not going to attempt to give a further detailed review of this particular period, first because it ended some 15 months ago and second because whatever I might say in that connection is available to members in the published report covering the operations of the Post Office Department.
In the year ending March 31, 1958, for which period the report has not yet been issued, the total postage receipts of the department amounted to $164,899,000, or an increase of $9,122,000 over the preceding year. In addition to these postage receipts the department enjoys revenue from a number of other sources, primarily fees on postal money orders, the rental of post office boxes and the payment from other countries for the handling of certain types of mail. The total of this revenue was $12,534,000, or an increase of $482,000 over the previous year; and with the inclusion of one or two minor adjustments representing $50,000 or so we arrive at the significant revenue figure for the Post Office Department for the year in question of $177,493,000, or an increase in total of $9,604,000 over the preceding year.
The department's disbursements for the same period totalled $177,893,000, or an increase of $15,843,000. Deducting the total disbursements from the total receipts the department therefore shows a net excess of disbursements over revenues of $399,901, and this compares with a net excess of receipts over disbursements to which I have already referred for the previous year of $5,780,471.
There are those who refer to this difference between the receipts of the department and its disbursements as the department's profit or loss on the year's operations, an assumption which is not strictly correct, because not included are such items as the cost of mail which is carried free for government departments, the cost of public buildings which are supplied free to the department by the Department of Public Works, and perhaps

Supply-Post Office
one or two other items. But the figure does provide a very adequate method of assessing the operations of the department.
Hon. members will have noticed a change in the department's net position from what might be termed a profit of $5,780,000 in 195657 to what might be termed the loss of some $400,000 in the year under discussion, and I should like to set forth the major reason for this change. Incidentally, these reasons were forecast some ten months ago in the last annual report of the department, which said:
It is advisable to draw attention to the fact that again in the coming fiscal year very heavy additional expenditures are in prospect-expenditures which are quite beyond the control of the Post Office Department.
The report then continued to outline these additional expenditures which have resulted in the figures which have been given to the house.
The largest single item of increased expenditure was in salaries paid to post office employees, $8,312,000 to our civil service staff proper plus $1,824,000 to revenue postmasters, making a total increase of $10,136,000. While a portion of this increase represented staff required by the increase in the volume of our business, the great majority, represented by some $7,500,000, resulted directly from the general civil service salary increases which became effective on May 1, 1957. An 11 per cent increase was also granted in January of 1957 to the railways in mail payments, and this is estimated to represent a cost increase of $1,250,000.
These two increases, totalling $8,750,000, could be added to in a great many cases, each representing an increased payment for exactly the same quantity of work performed or of goods and services received, and it becomes clear that even had the post office operations remained at exactly the same level as in previous years our previous favourable position would have been completely wiped out and would have been represented instead by a net loss of several million dollars.
In actual fact we did enjoy a substantial increase in the volume of our operations and this brought with it increased revenue. But increased revenue also brings with it increased expenditures, and these increases have been still further augmented by the natural growth of our country and the need to increase such postal services as rural mail routes and the like. Typical of such increases are those of $2,636,000 in salaries over and above the increase necessitated by the general salary revision, $2,036,000 for mail services by ordinary land conveyance, which includes the rural mail delivery, and an increase of $1,478,000 for mail service by air.

In addition, very briefly, there is another factor which was at work during the year under discussion, one which it is impossible to measure exactly but which we know affects the operations of the post office adversely at certain times as far as its revenues and expenditures are concerned. This is what we might call the revenue mix, and it relates to the various types of mail and the volume of each which is handled. It is important because certain classes of mail bring to the post office more revenue than others in relation to the cost of handling them. When business conditions become at all unsettled there is a certain falling off in first class profitable mail and a substantial increase in such comparatively unprofitable fields as third class mail, circular mail you may call it, since business firms begin to more actively solicit business by mailing advertisements, circulars, and the like.
Having reviewed the financial position of the Post Office Department over this period, I would like to summarize briefly the conclusions and then proceed to some other aspects of our operations. While the revenues of the department have increased, the expenses have increased at a faster rate in the year under discussion so that we are almost exactly at the breakeven point where revenues and expenses are equal. The increases in our expenses are due to factors over which the department has no control, such as cost increases for the same services performed and cost increases due to increased volume of work required. There is some evidence that the unprofitable types of mail increased in the year under discussion. The fact that cost increases totalling $8,750,000, from which the department enjoyed no advantage, could be absorbed and net revenue decline only $6,180,000 shows that in the year under discussion the department has operated at a substantially higher degree of efficiency than previously.
I would now like to turn to a review of specific aspects of our operation during the past year. In order to try to be as up to date as possible I will take the period from the beginning of July, 1957, to the end of June, 1958. In that period, of course, the most outstanding feature was the congress of the universal postal union. I must say that I have been touched greatly by the wonderful things which have been said about the organization and handling of that congress by the postal officials of so many countries in the world, both when they were here in Ottawa and subsequently when I met them or corresponded with them. Over 100 members of our staff were available for parttime work on various functions of this conference, working to arrange the details of

the operation. We are also grateful to the dozen or so other government departments which co-operated with us.
The congress itself included over 300 delegates from 96 member countries. Together they considered over 1,200 propositions relating to the various aspects of our international mail service.
Mr. Chairman, in connection with this congress it is only fair to say that the preliminary arrangements and planning had been made by the previous administration, and that this contributed greatly to the success of the congress. We took over at a period shortly before the congress started and were helped by that previous work.
I would like, Mr. Chairman, to pay a special tribute to Mr. Walter Turnbull, the deputy postmaster general for a number of years. He was elected president of the congress and he personally directed practically all its operations. He did an outstanding job in every respect.
I would just like to say another word about Mr. Turnbull. In 1956 he announced his intention to retire following the congress, and he carried out that plan. He was an outstanding postal official who contributed greatly not only to postal development in Canada but throughout the world as a result of his contacts with various postal administrations in every part of the globe. Not everyone was always in accord with Mr. Turnbull during his term as deputy postmaster general either inside this house or outside of it, but no one to my knowledge disputed his tremendous ability, intelligence and imagination as deputy postmaster general, and at his departure he left a Canadian postal service that in case after case bears the imprint of his own achievements.
Since we are on this subject, Mr. Turnbull's successor, to whom I paid tribute last year on the announcement of his appointment and to whom I will pay another tribute at this point since his appointment has become effective, is Mr. George Boyle, who has an intimate knowledge of the department gained over 43 years in its service during which time he has risen from one of the most minor positions to the highest permanent post in the department. In an organization which has so many excellent people from whom to choose, Mr. Boyle's progress is the best indication of his own ability, and already it is possible to see additional evidence of that in his new post.
I will have something more to say about the post office staff generally a little later, but I singled out these two men at this point because of my conviction that the Post Office Department is completely dependent upon the calibre of its personnel,
57071-3-1714
Supply-Post Office
and my feeling also that the type of man we have as deputy postmaster general is just one indication of the worth of that personnel.
Now, with respect to specific details and changes, over the last year door to door delivery was inaugurated in 10 cities serving 28,424 calls. In centres which already had this service it was extended beyond previous boundaries to add 48,342 calls, and in addition there was new service to 31,310 billed as "fill-ins" and calls falling within existing boundaries. The total number of new calls added under these three classes was 108,076.
While I am on the question of letter carrier delivery I might refer to two a day delivery, because this question of the return to two a day delivery of mail in the residential sections of our country where letter carrier service exists has often been discussed in this house. Hon. members will recall that it was abolished in 1952 by the previous administration.
In every aspect of postal service it is necessary to balance off those things which we might like to do against the cost of providing the service concerned, and these same considerations apply in this particular instance. In the last few years hours of work have decreased and rates of pay have increased, so that the resumption in residential areas of a second delivery a day at the present time would cost something in excess of $6 million a year.
In addition to the cost factor, conditions have changed in the past few years, with the result that a great deal more mail moving between cities is available for delivery in the cities of destination on the morning delivery, and also many arrangements of routes have been undertaken so that areas which faced particular problems at the change-over are now better served and more satisfied.
Over the years I have made a point of checking with people across this country on their reactions, and I have found that the average householder seems to feel that he is adequately served with one delivery a day, although business firms often find it an inconvenience when they are faced with that particular situation. I might just mention that such business firms and householders, if they are particularly interested, are in a position to obtain lock boxes at the local post office and thus pick up their mail several times a day.
Taking all these factors into consideration I have concluded that any general resumption of the two a day mail delivery in residential areas is not now warranted. However, every effort is being made to deal with

Supply-Post Office
local situations in a way satisfactory to individual patrons, and I am convinced that we can render satisfactory service in this way without the great increase of cost which would be entailed in the general resumption of two a day mail service.
In rural routes 74 rural routes were established to provide service to 11,500 patrons. In addition, 728 existing routes were extended to give service to 4,500 patrons. Twenty-eight revenue post offices were established in rural areas. Fifty-nine sub-offices and four new postal stations were opened in cities. To me a point of particular interest are the stamp vending machines, which many people find helpful. I feel that government stamp vending machines, which provide service 24 hours a day and give full value for the money inserted, are a great convenience to the public and therefore we are trebling the number available.
The choice of subjects and designs for postage stamps has been a subject of careful study, because we desire to produce stamps which will receive general approval of the public that uses them. Because stamp design is essentially a matter of aesthetics, and human tastes differ in that field perhaps more than in any other, we have to resign ourselves to the fact that it is unlikely that any stamp is ever going to be issued which will receive universal acclaim. However, steps are under way to establish an advisory committee on postage stamp design, because I feel that the views of a representative group of Canadians will be helpful in determining subjects and designs which will be most satisfactory to the majority of Canadians.
Because of changes in rail schedules and equipment which make it impractical to handle mail over certain routes where it used to travel, we have instituted additional highway services which are providing equal or superior connections.
Recently our regulations covering certain types of insertions in magazines and periodical publications were relaxed so that Canadian publishers might compete more successfully with publications coming into Canada from the United States.
During the year under discussion 55 new federal buildings were occupied by post offices, including two major projects, one in Vancouver and one in Winnipeg, which contain extensive mechanical mail handling equipment. One machine in operation at both Vancouver and Winnipeg is an electronic device for the sorting of parcels which is probably the most modern anywhere in the world. In addition to our new buildings, we have 16 additions to existing federal buildings, and we have 118 other projects in the planning stage.

Here is something which I think members might find interesting and perhaps have not heard about yet. Because all mail originates with the public, public co-operation and understanding of our problems are a vital necessity to successful postal operation. One way to achieve this co-operation is to keep the public well informed about the post office. We have therefore produced and issued a very fine moving picture in colour and sound in co-operation with the national film board. It is expected that millions of Canadians will see this moving picture over the next few years, and that it will result in a much better appreciation of our problems and more cooperation from the general public.
I turn now to our activities which concern more directly the internal operations of the department and the mechanical handling of mail. In previous years it seemed to me that the opportunity existed for closer co-operation among the United States, the United Kingdom and Canadian postal services in a number of fields. There has always been discussion of particular problems which concern the services in these three countries and, indeed, discussions with every country in the world wherever possible, but on no occasion in recent years until Canada took steps to initiate action have there been joint meetings of the most senior officials of the three services for a wide range of discussion of the general problems with which each was dealing and the plans for the future which each was developing.
Such an interchange of information is most important at a time like the present, when it seems apparent that we are entering a period of substantial development in mail handling operations. Over the past 40 years and until the present there has been substantially little development in the way mail has been handled in post offices. About the only general change, apart from one or two new types of machines in isolated cases, has been the introduction of moving belts and chutes to transfer mail from one location to another. Other operations have remained static and heavily dependent on the manual manipulation of each individual letter or parcel. This situation has applied in every country in the world, so it is no criticism of the Canadian postal service to point out that it exists in this country as well.
The primary difficulty in mechanizing and modernizing mail handling operations is, first, that large volumes of mail are found only in a limited number of locations and then only at relatively short peak periods, so that the installation of costly and complicated machinery to deal with such situations requires economic calculations and decisions of considerable complexity. On the technical side

the development of the necessary machinery, much of which is of an electronic nature, presents again very substantial difficulties. Most mass production operations deal with a standardized product. The mail stream varies widely, with each unit having the possibility of differing from every other unit in such respects as the size of the envelope, the position and denomination of the stamp, the thickness of the enclosure and the ultimate destination which is involved.
As a result, while highly qualified research technicians have been at work in a number of countries, including Canada, the United States and Great Britain, for a number of years trying to develop machinery which will handle mail more effectively and more expeditiously than at present, it is only in recent months that anything has begun to appear which, when put into operation in a post office in the regular mail stream, operates in a satisfactory manner. All of these facts and a great many more, all of which have been helpful in making progress in this respect-

Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman; about another ten minutes should cover it. I regret that we have 15 months to cover since the last annual report. All these facts to which I have referred were discussed at a series of meetings which have been held during the last year between Canada, the United States and Great Britain. One of the results of these meetings has been to convince us in Canada that the British post office has developed certain types of machines which should be of great help to us in this country, and we are in the final stages of discussion to enable us to instal prototype units of this equipment so that we may examine them under Canadian operating conditions and determine how extensively they may be used in our country. What our course of action will be after that I do not know, but certainly we should examine and study means which we feel are now available to speed and improve our mail delivery.
I have no doubt that within the next four to five years we will see the commencement of radical changes in mail handling techniques, and that within the next decade these same techniques will be widely employed in our Canadian postal service. In introducing them our prime purpose is to speed up and make more effective the handling of large volumes of mail, and to introduce machinery for certain laborious and unskilled post office
Supply-Post Office
tasks. It cannot be anticipated that this machinery will make any appreciable reduction in our permanent personnel, first because many of our jobs represent work which can never be mechanized-letter carriers are a good example-and second because the steady increase in volume of mail now demands a steady increase in our personnel, and the purpose of the machinery is to allow us to handle a larger volume of mail more quickly and effectively with the same number of people.
I should like to say a word about our own major project in the Canadian postal service. It is the electronic sortation machine on which close to $3 million has now been spent for research and development. The basic concept of the machine shows promise, but at no point up to the present could it be said that the machine is anywhere near the point at which it might be placed, even on a trial basis, in a post office to test it on regular mail for any extended period of time. I think that point should be made quite clear, Mr. Chairman. We are currently engaged in a very careful reassessment of this machine to determine our future course of action so far as it is concerned.
May I say a few words now about staff management, which is of interest to many members of the house. The general personnel policy of the Post Office Department, including staff training and development, is a well advanced and creditable one. As part of the department's program of management development, there was a marked increase in the number of officers and supervisors who rotated jobs or were assigned temporarily to other locations for varying periods according to individual needs. In this way we secured an interchange of ideas and information between headquarters and the field which is tremendously valuable in a widely extended operation such as our department.
A series of coloured slide films was produced within the department to give an over-all picture of the postal service and to acquaint our headquarters staff with postal operations, as well as to help indoctrinate new employees. We also use these slide films as visual aids to training.
We started in recent periods an accident prevention program in the Montreal post office. This resulted in such a substantial reduction in the number of accidents and the number of days lost as a result of accidents that the program was extended to the Toronto and Ottawa post offices.
We decentralized still further, giving the senior field officers wider authority for leaves. Headquarters no longer maintains individual records of staff for the larger field offices, nor any personnel records at all for part-time

Supply-Post Office
employees in the larger offices. This reduced the records staff at headquarters without any corresponding increase in the field.
The usual pattern continued of a percentage increase in staff of about half the percentage increase in the volume of mail. The turnover in our staff showed a moderate drop from 11 per cent to 9 per cent per annum. During the period I am reviewing the remuneration of 594 mail service contracts was adjusted upward to offset increased operating expenses and to bring the rates to a level comparable with those paid for similar work.
One of the heaviest burdens on our letter carriers is what is known as household circulars. A change has allowed these to be delivered on Monday as well as other days in the week, and this has spread the load to the advantage of the letter carriers and improved the service to the mailers.
What did the minister call that?

Householder circulars; a type of third class mail which the postman drops in at each house at which he calls.
To meet the constant problem of quickly providing suitable uniforms to new employees a change was made in the method of ordering and stocking them. It seems to me that this will improve both the appearance and morale of the new members of the uniformed staff.
Very special attention has been given to safeguarding the cash and postal values, particularly in the face of a substantial increase in the number of burglaries throughout the country, which applies incidentally not only to the Post Office Department but to other sections of the economy as well. Additional burglar alarms have been installed and additional safes have been supplied. More use is being made of night depositories in banks and other security measures have been introduced, designed to offer the maximum protection to the public whose valuables we hold.
Inquiries, which improve the post office service because they enable us to locate possible weaknesses and correct them, are being more effectively analysed and followed up on a national basis. We have established a more uniform system of processing them.
We have a work management program which involves the measurement of mail volumes processed, hours worked, and in most cases work standards. During this period the program was extended from certain major sections of eight of our largest offices to two additional offices.
It seems to me this is a very important part of our operation, because the results of

the program make postmasters and supervisors aware of the salary costs of various sections of their offices. It assists them also in studying operational conditions from the point of view of more effective use of staff. Finally, it instils a spirit of teamwork amongst employees and an ambition to better production. I can recall going into a post office in Winnipeg on one of my inspection trips and finding a large blackboard there on which the previous week's results were posted. A spirit existed in that post office, and exists in many others, of teamwork and a sincere desire to do a little better next week to improve those figures.
Here at headquarters, I think members will be very interested to know, we have installed one of the most modern machines available, a Univac 120 in our financial branch. This is an electronic accounting machine which will process the post office savings bank accounts and reduce the routine clerical work in that connection. We also use it to process the salary payments to revenue postmasters. It is estimated that these two uses of the machine will save the department $26,000 per year. I might just mention, in case the question comes up later, that this has been achieved without laying off any individual affected by the installation of this machine. There is a turnover in the department, and these people have been absorbed in other capacities. They have been called for on other jobs. Whenever we think in terms of a machine we think also in terms of our staff and the need to protect them in their jobs and not deny work through the installation of such machines.
Intensive studies of our money order system are under way with a view to developing a system based on electronic accounting machines similar to those being developed for the American Bankers Association and the Canadian Bankers Association. Again, this would reduce the routine clerical work of the department. I might say that the money order forms were redesigned during the year, and just that one little change in redesigning the money order form reduced printing costs by approximately $10,000 a year. We have improved considerably the procedures for controlling costs of the many truck contracts for parcel post, street letter box collections and special delivery in our various city services.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in conclusion may I say just one word to express a general attitude. Personally, I have not felt it possible to perform my own job without a fairly detailed knowledge of the basic operations and conditions of my department in every part of Canada. For that reason I have covered

Canada from Newfoundland to British Columbia to obtain personal acquaintance with our department and the individuals who work for it. I tried to work that out quickly this morning, and find I travelled something close to 25,000 to 30,000 miles last year in the performance of that duty. Wherever I have gone I have taken the time to talk person-nally with post office employees at every level, particularly those employees at subordinate levels who never before had seen a postmaster general in their office or met him in any way.
There are eight regional postmasters' associations as well as a national association. I have attended conferences of six of these eight postmasters' associations and a national meeting as well. As to the other two, I have given an undertaking to be there at their next annual meeting. I have received representatives of our employee groups and discussed with them their problems and suggestions. Finally, I made some attempt to obtain comparative knowledge of other postal services in the world.
These subjective experiences lead me to certain objective conclusions. First, I feel that our Canadian postal service is generally the equal of any in the world and probably superior to most. We face peculiar problems in our country in this respect: a huge country with a comparatively small population which is widely distributed and with great density only in limited areas; long hauls for much of our mail; isolated areas which are difficult of access, and many other problems. We can therefore make no attempt to duplicate exactly in any part of Canada those services which some countries give under vastly different conditions.
None the less, I am firmly convinced that when all factors are taken into consideration the Canadian people enjoy a postal service as good as that anywhere in the world and probably better than that in most areas.
The greatest portion of the credit for this, Mr. Chairman, must go to the post office employees themselves. The reputation of a postal service is not achieved overnight or by some sweeping changes in policy. Rather, such reputation is the result of faithful service, faithfully performed by a host of individuals over a long period of time. I might say that the motto of the Canadian postal service is Servire populo, "To serve the People". That motto, that faithful public service, has been the case in the Canadian postal service and it continues to be the case. Fine buildings and good equipment, new plans and improved methods all contribute to our success but in the final analysis it is the individual postal employee, in whatever post
Supply-Post Office
he may be serving, who determines the effectiveness of our service.
I feel sure that I speak for every member of this house when I pay a tribute to the postal employees of Canada for their devotion to duty and the part they daily play so successfully in the operation of those basic channels of communication without which our modern society could not exist.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a word of thanks to the Postmaster General for his comments and his analysis of the situation. However, in summing up what he has said I regret to say that his statement, as with that of other ministers, concludes by indicating a deficit as usual, ft is far from being a break-even policy which he always advocated while he was the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace sitting in the opposition. He has had fine experience and shown great ability since he became a member of parliament. I think he was the official critic for the then opposition. He worked hard at the job, even making research all around the department and even having access to confidential reports which the minister at the time was good enough to let him examine. Certainly in the Woods and Gordon report he found many suggestions and many statements that were extremely useful to him, just as the report was useful during the time of the former postmaster general.
After reviewing what the minister has just said we must come to the conclusion that almost nothing of what he used to say or nothing of the statements and the suggestions made by him while he was only an opposition member of parliament has been implemented since he has assumed office as Postmaster General. I recall that in 1953, 1954 and 1955 he filled the pages of Hansard with declarations and statements with regard to two a day mail delivery. I do not see that anything has been done since he has been the minister of this department. I can recall full pages of declarations by the Postmaster General. For instance in 1954, as reported at page 1178 of Hansard, before he was Postmaster General but was the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, sitting in the opposition he said this:
Before I resume my seat I have just one further question. I should like to ask the minister when we in Notre Dame de Grace are going to get our second mail delivery a day.
This matter of two a day delivery of mail was a political issue during the last election. In every province and at every meeting the Tory party used that kind of political issue, making promises and commitments. Now that the Conservative party is in power, now that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is Postmaster General, we are receiving letters

Supply-Post Office
from all over Canada asking when the minister will put into effect the dozens of declarations and statements covering pages and pages of Hansard asking for two a day mail delivery. Nothing has been done. For instance, from Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, Mr. Wadden wrote to us asking when this implementation would take place.
I do not know what is going to happen if, with regard to everything the minister said while he was a member of parliament, sitting in the opposition nothing is implemented. We are going to lack confidence in the minister. At that time he was extremely efficient. Today, when he occupies the post of Postmaster General, he might realize that the situation is a little bit different. Let us consider, for instance, the increase in the cost of postage stamps from 4 cents to 5 cents. How many speeches did the minister make about that increase in the cost of postage stamps? It was a good thing to say during the electoral campaign. But now that my hon. friend and his party have obtained power, now that they have obtained responsibility, now that they have obtained a majority on account of issues of that kind, now that he is in a position to implement the commitments he has made for many years, we find that nothing has been done.
He just said that the Post Office Department is very efficient. Does he mean that in the course of two, three, four or five months every efficiency there is in the Post Office Department is the baby of the minister, or is the efficiency the result of the fact that the department was well administered previously and he is taking credit for what was done by the previous government? I do not know whether he used to talk black one day and white on another day. In 1954, as reported at page 1818 of Hansard, when he was only a member of parliament sitting on the opposition side, the minister said this:
-but I criticize in the very strongest terms the Postmaster General for his administration of the department, and for many of the ways in which it is administered under his direction.
Today, however, he says everything is in order, everything is in good condition. He has made declaration after declaration inside and outside of the house to that effect. On June 24, 1958 the Victoria Daily Times had this to say:
"Canadian postal department is second to none" Mr. Hamilton said, "and the common feeling that Ottawa is unaware of local problems has no basis "
On July 25 the Globe and Mail reported that the Postmaster General had said that his four weeks' experience on the job had shown him an organization which, basically, was working very efficiently. Was it those

four weeks of the Postmaster General's experience which made this department work efficiently? I doubt it, and I think he will admit that something was done before he came to office. A little further down it says:
Formerly a fierce critic of the decision to revert to once-daily delivery, Mr. Hamilton now believes that few householders expect or want the mailman to call more than once-
I do not know what is going to happen over the years, but it is obvious that the suggestions made by the Postmaster General have not been implemented, so we must conclude that this department was well administered by the former government and that the present Postmaster General is only continuing what was done in the past. In his statement this morning no mention was made of the suggestions which he himself put forward when he was a private member, such as the one with respect to burglar alarms.

The
hon. member must have been asleep.
Oh, no.
That was all covered in the statement.	.

But I would like to know from the Postmaster General how many burglar alarms have been installed since he took office and how many thefts have occurred in the same period, just so we may compare the difference between his administration and that of the former minister. All these questions in my opinion should be answered. There is another point which I would like to raise. While the minister said inside and outside the house that the former government should cut expenditures and should stop the waste and extravagance, the minister in his statement this morning made no mention of these matters. He had an opportunity today to tell the house and the country all about the extravagance and waste and poor administration in the past, and because he did not we must only conclude that he was talking-

I would not say that because it is not polite, but I am sure the minister knows my meaning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is quite polite.
Instead of cutting expenditures, however, he has increased them by $5,700,000; and if hon. members will look at the estimates they will see that every item is increased-
Wages of employees also.

-except departmental administration, which has decreased by $301,633. Of

course there was the expenditure on the universal postal conference which last year cost $250,000 and we had $255,000 for publicity and advertising and so on, but still the conclusion one must draw from these estimates is that instead of cutting expenditures, for whatever reason, we have an increase of $5,700,000.
The minister spoke about electronic sorters and all kinds of machinery installed in the department, saying that he had not cut the number of employees. This may be so, though he was not very definite about it. I gather that this move will not hurt too much, but I would like to know from the minister how many employees are replaced by these electronic machines. If they have not yet cut the number of employees they may very well do so, which will stop Canadians from working in the department. When there is unemployment all through the country I do not think this is the time for the government to put in hundreds and hundreds of electronic or mechanical machines. Maybe it is a mere coincidence, but in recent weeks the civil service commission has been sending back applications for jobs to the senders because they are no longer taking records of applicants for mail carriers or clerks in the department.
Because of these facts it looks as if there will not be an increase in the number of employees of the Post Office Department, and I would suggest to the minister that the department should keep a file of all applicants for jobs such as those I have outlined so that when a vacancy occurs these applicants may be notified of the holding of examinations, rather than having to follow the newspapers every day or look at the notices in the public buildings. The minister I am sure will agree that it is pretty hard for an unemployed man to go through all the public offices to see if there is a notice of a job available to him. This is an improvement which could be made in the Post Office Department, and it is one which was advocated by the minister himself. All these questions should be answered, and the house should be informed of the cost of these electronic machines and of the department's experience in using them.
I do not think I have any more to say on this item, but I will have some other comments to make with respect to other items of the estimates. If he cannot implement the promises he made and which he repeated in the house and outside during the election campaign, he should tell us it was only for fun, that he was not really aware of anything wrong and that he was just taking a chance. And I know the present Postmaster General is in a position to 57071-3-172
Supply-Post Office
say that, because he is honest and ready to comply with the truth and with the facts.

It is not my intention to speak for very long, Mr. Chairman, but I feel that on this first vote I must say a few words, mainly because the Postmaster General in introducing the discussion had one thing to say in particular. That was in part a comparison of his present position with the attitude he took while he was in opposition and, to some extent, a withdrawal of the criticisms which he had directed against the department in the past.
At the time of his criticisms, that is before June of last year, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace sat very close to me, right in the next row, and it is because of what he said then that I should like to ask him a question. What has happened under his administration since last June in comparison with what he said for four years when he sat two seats away from me? I do not have to refer to Hansard, because I well remember the speeches made during that period by the present Postmaster General. Time after time he talked about two-a-day deliveries. Where are they today, and why has he changed his viewpoint? May I ask whether it is because in opposition he was irresponsible but that in government he is responsible?
May I also draw attention to a point which, though of less importance, is one which meant a great deal to the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace in those days, when week after week, if there was ever a robbery of a post office, he got up on the orders of the day and referred to those robberies and wanted to know what was going on. I should like to ask the Postmaster General what has been the situation since he took office, and whether he has been able to give a greater degree of protection than his predecessors in office. I do not know why this matter was of such particular interest for years to the present Postmaster General, but it was. Perhaps he can now throw some new light on the subject.
May I also draw to the minister's attention the fact that when he was in opposition he felt that those who lived in small towns and villages should enjoy the same rights with regard to postal service as those living in large towns and cities. I should like to ask the Postmaster General, in view of this, what is the basic policy determining when a town may have home delivery of mail. I have received a great number of inquiries on this matter from British Columbia, but in recent days I have heard from the town of Tilbury in Ontario, and I have been sent an editorial from the Tilbury Times. I hope

Supply-Post Office
the Postmaster General will tell us what is the policy governing conditions when home delivery can be made.
In conclusion I come to the major point. Remembering the speeches which the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace made when he sat alongside me for four years on the costings of the department, and in particular his references to first class mail having to bear the cost of other classes of mail-
Just so that I may understand the question and answer it adequately, would the hon. member care to give me some reference to Hansard where this particular observation occurs?
Mr. Chairman, I have not those references here, but I am amazed that I should remember the hon. minister's speeches better than he does himself.
Perhaps over the lunch hour the hon. member would look up the reference, because I do not recall that there is anything in the record along the lines he has suggested.

Perhaps the hon. member would cast his mind back to the days when the previous government was making a change in the postal charges. Can he remember the days of discussion on that measure and the fight that was put up by the Conservative opposition at that time to resist those changes? Does the minister not remember his own remarks on that occasion?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
You
are talking now about variations in rates-

The hon. minister does me the honour of allowing me to think I remember his speeches better than he does. The important thing is the position that was taken at that time. According to the last report of the department the post office, though naturally, of course, a public service, is a money-making proposition. All I want to ask the Postmaster General to do is to remember the position he took toward this matter while in opposition, and his opposition to first-class mail having to bear the heavy deficits incurred on other classes of mail of an industrial or advertising nature.
I merely draw this to the attention of the committee, and ask that during the course of this debate the Postmaster General will take the opportunity to outline the policies of the department in relation to the points I have sought to raise.

Mr. Chairman, the Postmaster General opened the discussion on this item by congratulating himself on his great good fortune in not having to deal with the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. I think

enough has been said already to prove to the Postmaster General that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is going to be quite a source of embarrassment to the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace as Postmaster General.
I remember-I think we all do-that when the Postmaster General was on this side of the house he waxed very eloquent about numerous subjects. Among them were the two-a-day mail delivery, government public relations, postal surpluses, and other things almost too numerous to mention. It may be interesting to hear what the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace had to say about the two-a-day mail service when he was on this side of the house, and I am reading from Hansard of May 26, 1955, at page 4146:
We know there Is no use complaining because it is going to be crammed down our throats anyway. I think that has been the attitude of the people of Canada toward this one-a-day mail delivery. I suggest this thought in that connection to the Postmaster General. Why do we not have two-a-day mail deliveries five days a week? At the present time we give a mail delivery in most residential areas once a day, and that is six deliveries a week.
Then again, on January 20, 1956, at page 362 of Hansard, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is reported as having said:
I should like to ask again, as I did last year, that the post office consider the re-establishment of the two-a-day mail delivery rather than the present one-a-day system which extends into such a large part of Canada. We should have a two-a-day mail delivery on a five-day week basis. I would point out that the return to the two-a-day, five-days-a-week delivery would not cause a major cost increase in the operation of the post office.
Again on May 26, 1955, at page 4146 of Hansard, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace is reported as follows:
I should like to say a few words about twice-a-day mail deliveries. I do not agree with the attitude of the Postmaster General and the department that once-a-day mail delivery is genuinely satisfactory or acceptable to the people of Canada.
Well, Mr. Chairman, that was the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace speaking as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. Contrast that with what the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace said this morning when speaking as Postmaster General. I did not have time to take down the exact words he used, but he did say that in considering the expression of two-a-day mail delivery we must balance what we would like to have against the cost of the service concerned, and he went on to say that this extra service would cost upwards of $6 million extra to the people of Canada but he did not stop there. He went on to say that he now believed that the one-a-day delivery was generally acceptable to the people of Canada, that the people were being

adequately served with one-a-day mail delivery and that the second delivery would not be warranted.
When we compare what the Postmaster General said this morning with what he said on this side of the house we must come to the conclusion that he has learned a great deal since assuming the burdens of office.
Thank you; those are the kindest words that have been said this morning.
He had so much to learn.

No member of parliament was more caustic in his criticism than the Postmaster General when he was just plain hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, and he used to wax loud, long and eloquent on the waste and extravagance of the Post Office Department. Yet when we look at the estimates for this year we find that they have increased by $5,786,390 over last year despite the fact that in 1957-58 there was $250,000 in the estimates for the universal postal union congress, and in addition the 1957-58 estimates included an amount for the approximate requirement for increases in rates of pay, but there seems to be no item to take account of further increases in the rates of pay in the estimates for the present fiscal year. Along that line, Mr. Chairman, the Montreal Gazette of March 22, 1958 carried the following extract, which is attributed to the Postmaster General:
Interchange of jobs between executives of industry and government was urged here yesterday by Postmaster General Hamilton to help businessmen to understand why the government has to employ more people than private industry to do a given type and volume of work. "If we were able to have a change of officers between private industry and government departments, both would benefit and derive greater respect for the other", Mr. Hamilton told members of the Montreal chapter society for advancement of management. The absence of the profit motive and the element of competition was cited by Mr. Hamilton as one of the "valid reasons" why government operations cannot equal the efficiency of private enterprise or its speed of adaptation to changing conditions. "The government has found it necessary to employ certain measures which may seem like empire building or unnecessary red tape to the men engaged in private enterprise, but which are actually needed to replace control by profit and competition", he declared.
The Postmaster General should tell us whether this is the answer to the accusation he used to make against the department "that it was full of waste and inefficiency". Then as late as June 24 of this year, as reported in the Victoria Daily Times, the Postmaster General is quoted as saying:
"Canadian postal department is second to none", Mr. Hamilton said, "and the common feeling that Ottawa is unaware of local problems has no basis." 57071-3-1724
Supply-Post Office
Does this mean that the Postmaster General is convinced that in recent years his department is and always has been efficiently run? The recent information that we have big brother listening in on our deliberations in the chamber calls to mind that several years ago the hon. member for Peterborough raised a very strong complaint about the use of television circuits in the post office in Peterborough. I believe he complained that there were 16 of them. I now have his exact words. As found on page 155 of Hansard for January 16, 1956, the hon. member for Peterborough said:
I understand that some 16 of these television cameras are to be installed in the Peterborough post office. Some of them will be dummies. In the past the men have never objected very much to the use of peepholes in post offices through which inspectors can watch and check on a man whom they suspect of not being honest, but they certainly do object to television cameras. Personally I think it is a waste of the taxpayer's money. It is going to cost over $50,000 to instal them, and will cause a great deal of hard feeling. The sooner the idea is thrown out by the Post Office Department the better for this country.
As late as yesterday, July 25, an inquiry revealed that this equipment is still installed in the Peterborough office. It was understood that it was installed on an experimental basis for a trial period. Perhaps the Postmaster General can now tell the house his conclusions as to its usefulness and if he thinks it is superior to the system of peepholes and observation galleries. Perhaps if experience warrants it we might improve the equipment in the Prime Minister's office and modernize it still further by installing a closed television circuit.
There are many things that I think would be very entertaining to us and very embarrassing to the Postmaster General, but I must desist from this pleasant occupation in order to deal with matters which are more urgent and pressing in the province from which I come. The first matter I wish to deal with is the position of revenue postmasters in Newfoundland. The Post Office Department report for 1957 lists 636 post offices in operation on March 31, 1956. It does not give any breakdown to indicate how many are staff post offices or semi-staff post offices, but I would assume that between 400 and 500 or approximately 75 per cent would be revenue post offices and that in the majority of these the postmasters would, in addition to their postal duties, have to carry out duties on behalf of Canadian National Telegraphs.
I have already referred to the plight of the postmaster-telegrapher in the house on many occasions, and I am not going to repeat what I have said before. My latest reference to the matter was on May 19 of this year, and

Supply-Post Office
earlier references in detail can be found on page 2235 of Hansard for April 20, 1951, and page 442 of Hansard for January 23, 1956.
The reason I bring the subject forward now is that Canadian National Telegraphs have recently made a decision, now in process of being carried out, to convert the equipment in these combined postal and telegraph offices from wireless telegraph to radiotelephone. As a result of that change many postmasters have suffered a serious decrease in that portion of their salaries which was paid by Canadian National Telegraphs, and the urgent question in the minds of all these people is, what is the Post Office Department going to do about it?
The Post Office Department cannot escape responsibility in this matter, because they worked out an agreement with Canadian National Telegraphs whereby they rented the services of these postmasters to Canadian National Telegraphs, and having done that they therefore made themselves responsible for the duties of these people and part of their remuneration; as a matter of fact the whole of their remuneration, because their cheques are received from the Post Office Department. I understand that the Post Office Department in turn has collected varying amounts from Canadian National Telegraphs in proportion to the services rendered.
This is an urgent matter because it concerns the welfare of human beings who, because of this action on the part of Canadian National Telegraph, have had their remuneration cut below a subsistence level. They are now on a starvation wage and, as I have pointed out before, hon. members must keep in mind that they cannot be compared with their prototypes on the mainland because many of them work in a separate building away from their places of residence and must be there during certain hours to answer calls and maintain a schedule of communication between the various C.N.T. offices. Therefore, even if they have to transmit their messages by telephone instead of by Morse code, the fact remains that their services are the same. Their time is tied up, and something must be done about their salaries. When the minister replies I hope he will give a full and detailed account of what the Post Office Department is planning to do with respect to this problem.
The second vital matter I want to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General concerns a recent order affecting some post offices in the rural outport communities of Newfoundland. This order stems from section 8 of the Post Office Act. That section has two parts. Part 1 reads as follows:

Except as provided in subsection (2), the Postmaster General has the sole and exclusive privilege of collecting, conveying and delivering letters within Canada.
Subsection 2 reads as follows:
The exclusive privilege referred to in subsection (1) does not apply to
(a)	letters carried by a friend on his way, journey or travel, if such letters are delivered by such friend to the addressee;
(d) letters lawfully brought into Canada and immediately posted at the nearest post office;
This section 8 of the act is amplified in the "Canada Official Postal Guide, 1957", page 108, under the general heading "General Laws and Regulations". On this page we find section 411 entitled "Postmaster General's Exclusive Privilege". I quote:
The Postmaster General has the sole and exclusive privilege of conveying, receiving, collecting, sending and delivering letters within Canada; and (except in the cases hereinafter mentioned) any person who collects, sends, conveys or delivers or undertakes to convey, or deliver, any letter within Canada, or who receives, or has in his possession any letter for the purpose of conveying or delivering it, otherwise than in conformity with the Post Office Act, for each and every letter so unlawfully conveyed or undertaken to be conveyed, received, delivered or found in his possession, is liable to a fine not exceeding $100 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two months or to both fine and imprisonment.
Then follow the exceptions:
The following are the excepted cases:-
(a)	Letters carried by a friend on his way, journey or travel, if such letters are delivered by such friend to the addressee;
(b)	Letters concerning the private affairs of the sender or addressee when sent casually by a messenger;
(c)	Commissions, affidavits, writs, processes or proceedings issued by a court of justice;
(d)	Letters lawfully brought into Canada and immediately posted at the nearest post office;
(e)	Letters of merchants, owners of vessels of merchandise, or owners of the cargo or loading therein, when carried by such vessel or by any person employed by such owners and delivered to the respective addressees, without pay, reward, advantage or profit for so doing;
(f)	Letters concerning goods or merchandise to be delivered with the goods to which such letters relate, carried by common known carriers without reward, profit or advantage for receiving or delivering them.
But the Post Office Act does not authorize any person to collect any such excepted letters for the purpose of sending or conveying them as aforesaid, nor does it oblige any person to send any newspaper, pamphlet or printed matter by post.
It will be seen, Mr. Chairman, that this section places tremendous powers in the hands of the Postmaster General to interfere with the private rights and liberties of the individual. I have received complaints from some of my communities that they have now been ordered that they cannot post any mail outside their own community where post offices exist or other than at the nearest post office. When we consider that in most of

these communities the frequency of mail service is once a week at the best and often once every ten days, it will be seen how handicapped the people of these places are, particularly the people who are trying to do business in these places, by not being able to send their letters to another post office where speedier mail service is available.
One complaint I received covered a businessman who lives in a community which has mail service once every eight days. He operates a boat from his community to Port aux Basques, which has a daily service, but he is not permitted to take his own letters on his own boat from his community and post them in Port aux Basques, where he can avail himself of a daily mail service. Surely this is a tremendous interference with the rights and liberties of that person, apart from the handicap it imposes upon him in the operation of his business. When I received that letter of complaint I could not believe that this order had gone out. I thought there must be some misunderstanding about it. However, since then I have received letters from other people complaining about the same thing.
Amongst these complaints we get some like this. A person may be in a certain community where the office closes at six o'clock. A taxi may be going to another community that evening or going to St. John's, where there is an air mail service. According to this regulation that person is forbidden to give the mail to that taximan to post for him in St. John's, where he could avail himself of better service.
I feel there is something wrong with this regulation, because certainly the mail is the property of the person who owns it and does not become the property of the post office until it is posted in the office. In any case, what is a letter? Does a letter become a letter merely because it is in an envelope and sealed? How do you distinguish between a letter and a note? I do hope the Postmaster General will look into this situation and give the house a detailed report on exactly what the order was that emanated from the post office in St. John's and went to these outport communities. What is his interpretation of the points I have raised in this discussion?
I see it is about one o'clock and I have another item to discuss. Perhaps I might call it one o'clock, because I notice my time is nearly up, so I will wait for another opportunity to discuss the other item.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONFERRING OF STYLE AND DIGNITY OF PRINCE OF WALES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the house for this opportunity. On this historic occasion I am happy to announce that Her Gracious Majesty the Queen has this day designated Prince Charles as Prince of Wales. It was particularly appropriate that the announcement was made at Cardiff, Wales, where today are taking place the concluding ceremonies of the British Empire games at which representatives of 35 nations within the commonwealth have been engaged in competition while their respective countries are joined in the co-operation which the commonwealth concept makes possible.
As I said a moment ago, the title is an historic one. It carries back the history of those in the British tradition to 657 years ago when Edward I created his eldest living son, Edward, the Prince of Wales, by letters patent. Since that date there have been 19 holders of the honour. During the period there have been long breaks during which no one held the position of Prince of Wales, the longest of which was following the elevation of Prince Hal to the throne as Henry VIII. One hundred and one years passed after Prince Charles, afterward Charles II, ascended the throne. For a period of 54 years no one held this honour.
It is now 22 years since there has been a Prince of Wales, the last being Edward VIII who had the honour conferred upon him on his sixteenth birthday in June of 1910.
I think that all of us would at this time desire to express our congratulations to the Prince of Wales who, in the process of the fulfilment of God's will, will ultimately occupy the throne. To Her Majesty the Queen I am sure all hon. members would desire to convey their good wishes coupled with the hope that her health may soon be fully restored. As to the Prince of Wales, I think I can do no better than quote the words of the poet:
Among our ancient mountains,
And from our lovely vales,
Oh, let the prayer re-echo:
"God bless the Prince of Wales!"

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house rejoice in the announcement which has just now been made by the Prime Minister that Her Majesty the Queen has seen fit to confer upon young Prince Charles the title of Prince of Wales. We rejoice also because, as the Prime Minister has said, this title has been vacant now for many years. We have watched with joy and interest the life of this young boy as he has been growing in strength and wisdom. I am sure that all of us on this side of the house would wish to associate ourselves with the words of the Prime Minister in congratulating the young prince upon this honour. I should like to add that I hope and trust that Almighty God will not only support him in his young years but will also guide his life so that the destiny which one day will fall upon him will be a source of consolation not only to the members of the royal family but a source of strength for those who form part of the British commonwealth of nations.
