speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group realize that under our form of government, our constitution, our basic rights and freedoms are vested in the crown. We were very much interested to hear the announcement made by the Prime Minister just now. We trust that this young man will continue to have good health and much happiness as a result of being a prominent personage in a commonwealth working toward greater freedom, greater happiness and peace for all people in the world.

The house resumed in committee of supply, Mr. Rea in the chair.
304. Departmental Administration, $1,886,095.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to be quite brief in my opening remarks on these estimates. However, I want to make a few general remarks before we proceed to the items. Then when we come to the items I have some questions to ask relating to administration and some matters of more or less parochial interest to my constituents.
When I address the minister as Postmaster General, I think he should really be addressed as the minister of successful social enterprise. As a result of the precedents established by him when he was a member of the opposition, -he, in fact, I think on one occasion being almost solely responsible for holding up the postmaster general's estimates for two
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
days-I trust that he will not object to a very close and lengthy study of his estimates at this time.
Having said that, I want to express my appreciation of the prompt manner in which the minister has dealt with any matters which I have brought to his attention and also of the courtesy of the senior officials, whether in Ottawa or in Vancouver, in their close attention to any worth-while complaint that is directed towards them. Furthermore, we should all express our gratitude to the great multitude of humble civil servants who stamp the letters; run the post offices; deliver the mail in our cities, towns and villages; and carry on the service on our rural mail routes. If it were not for this co-operation extending right from the rank and file of the organization to the minister we would not have the successful administration of postal affairs that exists today.
I noticed what the minister had to say when he was making his statement this morning and I, for one, as I think did the other members of this group, appreciated his making a full statement with respect to the administration of his department, particularly in view of the fact that the latest report we have is the one dated March 31, 1957. I understand from my experience in this house that the report of the Post Office Department does not usually come out until the fall. I might say in passing that I do hope, as one interested in stamps, that this will be the last edition of any report published by the post office which carries the picture of that gloomy goat, because I have lived very close to a lot of goats and I have never in my life seen such a caricature.
I was particularly interested in three matters raised by the minister, first of all the question of public relations, and I was very pleased to hear his reference to that topic because I think the successful administration of his department depends to a great extent on satisfactory public relations. I realize the work that has been done in the large centres in that respect and the attendance of the minister and his officials at such public events as fairs, and my only further suggestion is that these public relations activities be extended to the smaller centres as much as possible. As a matter of fact some of the, shall I say, complaints, arise from the smaller places because of a lack of understanding of the department's administration and so on, and I do suggest that his officials conduct these public relations activities in those smaller centres to a greater extent than has been the practice in the past so that the people there will have the same opportunity to understand the administration as

the people in larger centres. I am one, as you know, Mr. Chairman, who has always urged consideration of these people who live in the smaller communities and the more isolated spots in our country.
I was also very pleased to hear the minister's reference to an advisory committee with respect to the choosing of designs for stamps. I think we have been very backward in this respect in Canada, especially when I look at some of the most beautiful stamps issued by little Oriental states and small nations elsewhere and by what we consider undeveloped and in some cases backward states. With respect to stamps we in this country have to date a lot to learn, and I am very glad the minister has suggested this advisory committee so as to get, shall I say, the viewpoints of numbers of people interested in this art. It is another illustration of the development of the collective principle within his department-not the "great wise man" but the collective wisdom of a number of people-it is another aspect of the C.C.F. policy being put into practice by the government.
Another matter I would like to mention particularly is that in recent years-and I think this is a very good practice-the departmental officials have somewhat changed their approach with respect to replies to applications for mail services or changes in mail routes and things of that sort. A few years ago one would get a rather cryptic letter from the department in reply to such an application to the effect that "the matter has been under consideration and the decision is in the negative" or something equally as cold blooded. I now find that on a number of occasions departmental officials are giving reasons and by way of illustration may I say that in my district some years ago there was quite a demand for changes of a mail service. From a local point of view this seemed pretty reasonable, especially in some cases where a certain mail service would appear to have a shorter route as a result of such an application being granted, but sometimes people are not acquainted with the economic factors involved. The particular instance of which I am thinking happened some years ago and the departmental officials gave me a thorough explanation of the costs involved and the reasons why it was not economic to accede to the wishes of the local people. I do suggest to the minister that when dealing with a lot of these questions a great deal of discontent and unnecessary correspondence might be avoided by some detailed explanation as to the basis upon which a decision is reached.
Supply-Post Office
I mention this matter because I was very taken with the fact that when this application was first presented there was a lot of local heat but in some cases not very much light because they did not understand the situation. However, when I got the explanation in a somewhat lengthy letter those people who had been most active in the matter readily understood the situation and the basis for the department's decision.
Before the minister's estimates are concluded and when he replies to our various complaints on item 1 I wish he would give to the house a very brief summary of the types of post offices which exist within his department; that is to say the classifications and terms of employment for each type of post office. I am particularly concerned with the way the post office operates and the postmasters' salaries, some of which are covered by revenue from stamps and things of that sort, particularly with respect of the rights of the postmaster in regard to the employment of help. For instance, does the veterans' preference apply with reference to employment of help by postmasters of this revenue classification, and if competent citizens are available do they receive preference over noncitizens, and so on? I mention these matters because they have been brought to my attention on a few occasions.
I am also particularly concerned with payments to postmasters, particularly in small post offices and the usual regulations in respect of the administration of these post offices. For instance I would like the Postmaster General to tell us how many hours a day or how many days a week such a post office is required to keep open and if the minister could, when he replies, give an outline of classifications and terms of employment in each type of post office, I would appreciate that very much, although I am not suggesting he should go into any great detail.
Those are my few brief opening remarks. Later on I shall, after consideration of the minister's estimates, co-operate with anyone who is willing in order to demonstrate to the minister that we have an equal capacity to deal with estimates as he had when he was in the opposition.

You
have already demonstrated that.

This morning the minister informed the committee that an advisory committee would be set up to help the minister with respect to the design of stamps. We do hope that the minister does not for a moment think that if in the future a committee is to advise him on these designs that he can hide behind that committee. We

Supply-Post Office
will hold the minister responsible as he held the previous postmasters general responsible.
I would like to make one suggestion to the minister before he sets up this committee. I do hope all the provinces will be represented including, of course, the province of Quebec, so that when new stamps are issued to celebrate historic events all the provinces will be brought into the picture.
I have a few remarks to make on a subject which was the topic of previous speeches heard in this committee this morning and having to do, of course, with the numerous statements and promises made by the Postmaster General in connection with the reestablishment of a second mail delivery a day. This was more than a promise, it was a commitment and a solemn one, and at the time this commitment was made the Postmaster General was the spokesman for his party on matters having to do with the post office and he was therefore representing the views of his party. Then, to add insult to injury, on July 25, 1957 the Windsor Star reported that the Postmaster General had reiterated after the first election of his party that he would re-establish the twice a day delivery service.
We are awaiting a statement by the Postmaster General with the greatest interest, because he has completely failed to give us a proper reason for the change of policy of his party in this matter, and when we talk about Conservative policies unfilled we will always remember the bluff of the two deliveries a day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Listening to the remarks that have been made this morning and this afternoon by the Postmaster General I draw the conclusion that the Postmaster General's statements previously were not in keeping with the operation of the department.
I draw the inference also from the fact that I looked up to find what the Postmaster General's report was-I find that this report, the last one endorsed by the present Postmaster General-published in March, 1957, and having observed the lag in time from the time that report is prepared to the time it is presented, I presume that the Postmaster General was, in effect, in this particular case, endorsing the program the Liberal government had already implemented with very little change. I think the Canadian people should take a good deal of interest in the department because this is one of the large departments of government. We find that while hon. members were in opposition certain considerations were raised and certain suggestions made, but when the opposition has formed the government there are very
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
few changes. Unless the report which I think should legitimately have been published before this was discussed shows the contrary, we can only draw the conclusion that there has been very little change.
I should like to question the Postmaster General on the matter raised by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo this morning regarding these television snoopers that were installed several years ago in Peterborough. He mentioned the fact that he was very much opposed to this. This certainly was the opinion expressed by the hon. member for that constituency while he sat in opposition, and I think I would like to go further still and say we not only object to these television cameras being installed but, also, that they should remove the people who inspect the work of this department from observation galleries. Knowing, Mr. Chairman, the examinations that the people in the post office must take, the responsible positions they have to assume and the very satisfactory operation and performance of their duties by the post office officials across the country, I do not think, legitimately, we should allow any snooping, and certainly we are very much opposed to this television aspect of examining the work of people. We have had no reason for this type of investigation. Certainly I think a much more satisfactory method of supervising this work could be devised, and the minister might consider the bonding of employees.
Another matter which has been raised in the past, and this is one in which I hope the Conservative regime does not make a change, is the post office savings bank. Many hon. members may not have had any experience with this bank, but I would suggest that this is a very valuable service which the post office has performed which it should be proud of and advertise more. While it is true many of the small post offices do not want to be bothered with this, it is advantageous to the travelling public of Canada, such as salesmen and service personnel- that is the first time I came into contact with the post office savings bank, in the air force *-and it means you can deposit money any time the post office is open, up to six o'clock. It is a great establishment for anybody moving from town to town where they are not too well known, because all you have to do is take your book into any post office and if there is any money indicated on your card you can receive that money in almost every small town across Canada. It means you do not have to go through the formalities of phoning a bank to check on your home account; you do not have to carry travellers cheques, and it seems to me a great service

would be accomplished to more Canadians if the Canadian people were better advised on the operations of this bank.
I am quite sure that the Postmaster General is going to give a complete report on the financial position of the bank and I would strongly urge that he give some consideration to extending the services rather than curtailing them. We are well aware of the fact that some of the banks and other institutions in the financial field are not too happy about the federal government operating this type of savings bank, but I would point out that it has been in existence in Britain for many years and is used in a similar manner to that in which the Canadian service personnel use it but on a much larger scale, and I think it is a great establishment.
Something has been said today about the institution of the two-delivery system for mail. While we are not opposed to this, we suggest there must be an extension of the mail delivery service particularly in small towns on a greater scale than is taking place today before we contemplate extending two-service delivery in the larger centres. We still have many small and medium sized towns that do not enjoy a door-to-door delivery such as many of us have come to accept and want extended, and until that is done I think we should continue on a program of extending this door-to-door delivery before we extend in the other fields.
There are probably 3,000 rural mail deliveries being made in my riding, and with this we have a bit of a problem. We have been led to believe over the years, probably by United States movies, the old story that the United States mail must go through whatever the weather conditions. Unfortunately that is not true in Canada. In my area there appears to have been no consideration given to those areas that may be snowed up in the wintertime. The contract is let on the basis that the mailman is able to drive his car around the route. He may not own a horse, and yet 15 or 20 miles of his route will be blocked for two or three months, and I think an additional sum of money must be inserted into his contract to allow him to make these rural deliveries to the places that weather hazards make impossible to be visited for the contract price he is receiving for delivery of mail by car.
I think it may have been romanticized a bit by United States movies, but I think the idea when we post a letter is that we expect it to get to its delivery point as soon as possible. But in many of the areas I am speaking of the mail is not delivered for weeks at a time, and is only delivered then when people go out to a small grocery store.
Supply-Post Office
It is not a post office by any means, but the mail is there, and they can pick up the mail at that time. The storekeeper does not receive any remuneration for his part in the delivery, and I think something could legitimately be done about this matter.
Another problem is the extension of rural deliveries. While it is, as I understand it, the policy of the Post Office Department on occasions to make extensions to existing rural routes, it is very difficult to get a completely new route set up. We have a number of communities that were at one time associated with a small village. The people went to that village for their groceries and they picked up their mail in the small grocery store. That situation has changed. The grocery store is gone. The people do not go to that small community store any more; in fact, in many instances it does not exist any longer. The small village in which I was born is a good example. At one time it was a very small metropolis and now it is not a centre of activity at all, and yet the people in that particular area are not on the extension of an existing mail route, nor can it be argued legitimately that they should be on any existing route because there is no extension; but on a number of occasions they have petitioned to have another rural route set up but they have not been successful.
Another problem we are having in northern Ontario has to do with the extension of the suburbs of many communities. The people in the suburbs are having great difficulty in getting post office boxes. If we could extend the door-to-door deliveries in those communities it would solve the problem. If we are not in a position to extend the deliveries at the present time, then it is necessary for the Post Office Department to put postal boxes in the area. I have noticed that in a number of cities in southern Ontario they have placed outdoor boxes on the street and a person can get a key for the box door and get his mail in that way. Places like Blind River and Elliot Lake have undergone a tremendous expansion program in the last few years. The mail service is very poor. It is impossible to get a box. The mail is delivered through general delivery and frankly I do not think that is an efficient way of handling mail where four or five thousand people have to come into the post office in a limited period of time. The practice of installing temporary boxes, if necessary, would go a long way toward alleviating some of the problems in that area.
I am also quite interested in the matter of stamps. At one time I collected stamps and I might point out that such places as Ghana, New Guinea, Togoland and so on,

Supply-Post Office
which are only to me place names, have produced some of the best looking stamps that have been printed. Although we do not have tropical scenery, we have much scenery that could be reproduced on stamps. We do not have to try to draw waves that look like straight lines or curved lines; we do not have to make that kind of stamp, but we can produce very valuable stamps and I should like to express our appreciation of the stamp that was designed to depict the mining industry of northern Ontario. This stamp was very favourably received in northern Ontario and it was a satisfactory stamp. I think it could have had a little more colour in it. We have a great deal of colour in northern Ontario and the stamp could have depicted some of that colour. The stamp that commemorated the paper industry was also commended. If we can do that with two or three stamps I do not see any reason why we could not depict many more scenes in colour, and we might sell more to the stamp collectors.
When the Postmaster General replies I hope he will refer to the matter of the savings bank and that he will comment favourably on the fact that we should extend the post office savings bank, particularly for the benefit of those people who are no longer able to drop into their home bank when they need money and when they are travelling on the road for a week or two. In those circumstances they can drop into the post office and pick up $50 or $75 and not have to call their home bank. I have had to do that on many occasions and sometimes when I made the telephone call there was not enough money in the bank to call about. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to remind the house of the fact that the constituency for which I sit was formerly represented by one of the predecessors of the present Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton), the Hon. Alcide Cote. Before beginning my remarks, I would very much like to remind the house of the excellent way in which the Hon. Alcide Cote discharged his duties at the time he was head of the department whose estimates are now under consideration.
The Hon. Alcide Cote was a man of deep honesty, a true democrat, a real servant of the people. Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, he was prematurely taken away from us, and I felt than on this occasion I should recall his memory in the house.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest this morning to the speech delivered by the Postmaster General. We in particular, in the constituency of St. Jean, have long known of the hon. gentleman, as the one who had been entrusted with the task of criticizing in this house his predecessor, the late Hon. Alcide Cote.
I wish to thank those of my colleagues who, this morning, recalled a number of instances of criticism offered by the hon. gentleman who, at the time, was just the member for Notre Dame de Grace. Hansard records so many speeches of his criticizing the Post Office Department that I believe I should briefly point out some of the statements found in those speeches. Mind you, I have no intention of reading all the vague and insignificant claims made at that time by the hon. gentleman. I certainly have no intention of quoting from the official record the criticism, complaints, lamentations and gnashing of teeth indulged in at the time by the present Postmaster General. He would refer to post office robberies as though they had been invented by the Liberals. He would speak of departmental waste and extravagance; of inefficiency in the postal system under the Liberal administration; and he used to say that it was the department's duty to restore twice a day mail delivery in Canada.
Well, Mr. Chairman, when we saw the Postmaster General rise in his place this morning, we did not quite expect the remarks he did make. We were expecting the minister, who had witnessed so many robberies, to come into this house dragging after him the thieves he had ferretted out in the course of his inspection tours throughout the country. We were quite surprised to hear from him the admission that he was the first Postmaster General since confederation-and I wish to emphasize that fact-who had visited every post office in the country up to and including Newfoundland. The statement deserves emphasis for, if the Postmaster General has visited so many post offices, it must be because he was looking for those evil spirits which, at the time, were supposed to haunt the Post Office Department.
Having gone from one post office to the next, having put questions and carried out investigations, he comes back before us, to tell us what? To say that the criticism, the sly claims he had made before parliament for five years were but the outcome of a

vision, to use a word which we have learned recently. We have it out of his own mouth, Mr. Chairman, that the postal system of this country, so well administered by the Liberals before him, compares favourably, he has found, with any other postal system in the world.
Let me therefore state at this point that, in making those remarks, the minister was not paying tribute to the present government; he was merely establishing that the preceding administration-the Liberal administration which he had so bitterly criticized-was not so bad after all but was thoroughly commendable.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to remind the minister of what he had said, as reported on page 1179 of the French version of Hansard for January 14, 1954. The minister (who was then member for Notre Dame de Grace), giving the house a review of the Department's financial situation since 1945, said:
"In 1953, there was a surplus of $6,470,000 (in round figures); in 1952 the surplus was $6,649,000; in 1951 there was an error-"
"-somebody made a mistake and there was a deficit of $1,327,000;-"
"And there was a deficit!"
Now, Mr. Chairman, the member for Notre Dame de Grace, when in opposition, used to wonder how there could be a deficit! Surely, he would say, there must be a mistake! Well, today we could rightfully ask him where the error was made for we see that there is still, definitely, a deficit. And if error there be, it was surely the one made by the electorate in choosing the Conservative party.
Mr. Chairman, the minister also referred to an electronic sorting device to improve the system and speed up the handling of mail throughout the country. Now, I deplore that the present Postmaster General should speak of electronic sorting, that he should talk of substituting machinery for manpower, just when we need to recruit as much manpower as possible to arrest the tide of unemployment which is rife throughout the country at present. I hope the Postmaster General will alter his policy, and thoroughly contemplate the implications of such changes before introducing them.
Mr. Chairman, I will put off some of my observations until we take up the various items. Howevea, I wish to associate myself with all the others in saying that the Postmaster General has totally betrayed the promises he made when he told the public that he would expose the scandals he used to talk about. We have only to refer to newspaper reports of the election campaign to find accounts of the infllammatory speeches of the present Postmaster General. He has not always been indulgent towards his opponents.
Supply-Post Office
Furthermore, let me quote page 4346 of Hansard of the 26th of May 1955. The following sentence Mr. Chairman, will show you the mentality of the Postmaster General when he was merely member for Notre Dame de Grace. Just listen to this:
"But sometimes it's possible to knock some sense even into a stupid Minister-"
That's what he said at the time.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is a reflection on his own even greater stupidity that, having spent five years criticizing others, he is now unable, having taken over from them, to put his finger on a single error of the government which was the butt of so many of his tirades. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, my remarks are going to be very brief. I want the Postmaster General to know how much the people of Brantford appreciate the work done by the local postmaster and his staff last weekend when the change-over took place from the old building to the new wing that has been opened. It was a good job, well organized and well carried out when you realize that service was given in the old building until Saturday noon and complete facilities for serving the public were transferred to the new wing and ready for service on Monday morning. I should also like to state that the people of Brantford appreciate the efforts of the former member for Brantford who was a member of the previous government and prevailed upon that government to start the addition into which the post office moved last week-end.
It is a splendid building and we are quite proud of it. It is a credit to the government and to the city of Brantford. We hope that when the complete job is finished and we have the re-opening ceremony the Postmaster General or the Minister of Public Works will come to Brantford and officiate because we would be very proud to have them in our city.
There is only one suggestion I should like to make to the Postmaster General. In my opinion, instead of creating double service in the larger cities we need to have service in the smaller centres and also to extend rural delivery service so that farmers who live some distance from their mail boxes will not have to travel anywhere from half a mile to a mile to the corner of the road in order to collect their mail. That is all I have to say.

Mr. Chairman, it has often been said that a person cannot quit a position, assume another and still have the same boss. As a former postmaster and supervisory postmaster for over 35 years I had the honour to work under the present Postmaster General for one year and now that

Supply-Post Office
I am a member of the house I feel that he is still one of my bosses. It was a privilege to work under his guidance, as well as that of other postmasters general, and I am happy to say that my welfare as a postal employee was always his first consideration. I have received co-operation from the Postmaster General and together with the assistance of the general public my position was a pleas ant one.
Post office business is a big business. I was impressed by the fine report given this morning by the head of the department. The change that has taken place during my 35 years as a postmaster is amazing. Air mail and all-up mail service have been probably one of the greatest achievements in post office history. I was glad to hear the Postmaster General state that even greater improvements are being made with regard to this type of mail. I may say that not very long ago in my post office a letter was mailed at 5.30 in the evening and at 9 o'clock the next morning a gentleman walked into the Halifax post office and the letter was there in general delivery.
The sortation of ten million letters daily by 12,000 post offices can give some idea of the great work being done by the department. The addition of area superintendents throughout the whole of Canada and also supervisory postmasters has helped to make today's service, as the Postmaster General put it, second to none in the world. Area superintendents, district directors, regional directors and heads of the department were ever ready to assist all employees in their many problems. This gave us the opportunity to serve John Public as civil servants in a courteous and efficient manner. Post office boxes in the lobby, boxes throughout the town and rural delivery have helped to give better service in smaller communities. I understand that house to house mail delivery can only be provided in places with a population approaching that of a city.
I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General that part time assistants be employed under the civil service commission in the same way as full time employees. I believe they would give still better service than they are giving at the present time and they would also have the opportunity to have superannuation to their credit on retirement. If this were done we would have a better opportunity to secure part time helpers.
Finally my observations over 35 years lead me to say that postal employees working under the civil service commission and under the fine leadership of the Postmaster General are making an outstanding contribution to the welfare of our great country and I think we are all proud of their fine record. I

am sure we can all say that our Post Office Department is second to none in the world.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly about the small salaries paid to postmasters in some of the more isolated places in Newfoundland. Actually, it is quite well known that in many cases these salaries are utterly inadequate. The surprising thing is that the government, which should lead in showing a proper appreciation for faithful service, has been so backward in allowing the scale of salaries to remain so low. I think everyone will agree with me when I say it is impossible for a man, his wife and family to live on the salary of $150 a month, and in many cases the remuneration is even lower.
The postmaster plays a very important part in isolated communities. He is one of the most important individuals living in that community. I hope the Postmaster General can find a way to reward him. I believe that up until recently postmasters' salaries were based upon the revenue of the post office. I have learned with a great deal of pleasure that the salaries now will be based upon the amount of work done rather than upon the amount of revenue which the office obtains. The thing that has to be done now is to make this unit value high enough.
I might also point out that the amount of rent paid for post office quarters in some instances is pitifully small.
I might mention, too, that in many areas of Labrador the mail service is poor and far from being what it should be. There are only a few places in which there are postmasters, and mail is landed from the coastal steamers only at those places. The result is that the people have to go for many miles in order to get the mail which has been dropped off by the coastal steamers. I would request that provision be made whereby mail will be dropped off at each port of call. As an illustration of what I am saying, I would point out that the mail for Port Hope Simpson is carried there on the steamer but is not landed there. It is taken on to Williams Harbour, 20 miles away, although the steamer has actually called at Port Hope Simpson. The people from Port Hope Simpson must chase the steamer 20 miles in order to get the mail. Then the steamer which calls at Green Bay does not have a mailman aboard. In the old days all the coastal steamers used to carry a mailman. Since this steamer does not have a mailman letters cannot be mailed aboard but they have to be carried to the nearest post office ashore. If a nurse wants to send a small parcel of medicine to a nearby community, she has to get a crew member or a passenger to carry it. The reinstitution of mail men aboard coastal steamers would be

a great public service and the cost involved would be small.
I should like to mention, too, that the Canadian National telegraph office and the post office should continue to be joint offices rather than separated. In the old days, the Canadian National telegraph operator was also the postmaster, and between the two positions could sometimes get a reasonable salary. There has been an effort to separate these offices, and this effort should cease. In fact, a countereffort should be made to make them joint offices operating under the same people and in the same building. While I am mentioning buildings, and before I sit down I hope that the Postmaster General will recommend the provision of post office buildings in Badger, Glenwood and Robert's Arm.

I was very pleased indeed to hear the minister's report this morning. I was particularly pleased to note the great pride that the minister took in his work, and in the work being performed by the post office. As the hon. member for Kootenay West pointed out, he is rapidly learning that public enterprise is workable and the people who work in a public enterprise are able to render a degree of efficient service that is equalled by no other. I noted particularly when he expressed the motto of the post office, that it was to serve the people. The motto is not to make money, not to make profit, but to serve the people. The minister did his utmost to convince us on this side that this public enterprise known as the post office was working. He used the phrase that it was functioning so smoothly, so efficiently, that our post office record was an outstanding one. I was pleased to note the compliment he paid the employees. It is often said that men must have the lash of the profit motive behind them; they must be able to see money; they must have every expectation of receiving a high monetary return, before they will exert their utmost effort.
I was very pleased when the minister referred to the former depuy postmaster general, who has spent a lifetime in public service by saying that case after case bore the imprint of his achievements. I think I have the wording right, but at least it is close. The minister expressed confidence that the new deputy minister will have an equally outstanding record of public service. Those of us who have met the new deputy minister from time to time know that the minister's confidence is going to be fulfilled.
I should like to call the minister's attention to a number of little matters which, to me, involves some principles. In the first place, I should like to refer to the suggestion of bonding the employees. I feel that
Supply-Post Office
would be rather unnecessary. I noticed that according to the annual report for 1956-57 there were only 335 prosecutions, and of those only 96 involved employees of the post office. Here again, Mr. Chairman, is a wonderful illustration of the ability of people to serve, even though the incentive to serve may not be monetary but rather one of serving people. I do not know, offhand, how many employees the post office has, but it likely runs into the tens of thousands.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: About 50,000.

The minister says, 50,000 and out of 50,000 people only 96 had to be prosecuted in one year for a whole host of wrong things, such as robbery, receiving, shortages, thefts, forgeries and so on. I think that speaks very well for our employees.
I should like to compliment the minister on the new atmosphere which prevails in his department from one end of Canada to the other on the part of everyone concerned. They make the public really feel that this is not some hierarchy of government, but this is the post office which belongs to the public and all the employees are actually public servants. I have only to compare the attitude of the minister with the attitude of other ministers to know that that is at least partly the wish of the minister that this new atmosphere ought to prevail. The success of any public enterprise depends very much on the attitude of the public being served towards that institution. If the public feels alienated in so far as that institution is concerned, if they feel that it is not part of them, they also do not feel any responsibility towards that institution and the efforts of that institution to serve the public are hampered.
I was hoping the minister would announce that henceforth regulations might play a slightly lesser role in his department. Every so often we run into regulations. Some of the requests of the people seem to be so logical and very often so minor and so simple yet they mean so much to the people concerned that they cannot understand the need for detailed regulations. I know that when there is danger of a bureaucracy in any institution, whether privately-owned or publicly-owned, you build up regulations. Every time something goes wrong some official thinks up a new regulation that ought to be put into effect. Without having regard to the small number of things that do go wrong, in an effort possibly to avoid a repetition of a wrong, out comes a new regulation.
I have in mind such regulations as that as to the hours at which wickets can be kept open in a major post office in one of

Supply-Post Office
our large Canadian cities. Surely at a post office such as in Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver-and I am now referring to the main post offices-where they have hundreds and hundreds of employees, it should be possible, by rearranging of employee hours, to keep wickets open right around the clock. I do not suggest that all the wickets should be kept open but some of the wickets might be kept open. However, on some afternoons I have found some wickets closed in large post offices. I believe that statement is correct, if my memory serves me rightly and unless there has been a change since then.
I know the origin of this regulation. It originated from the principle of the 40-hour week. However, there is no reason why the men cannot have a 40-hour week in a large post office and yet some wickets and some service be available to the public at all hours. Working people working regular hours in Canada-which ordinarily means that after breakfast they begin work and they come home for dinner at six o'clock at night-find it extremely hard to use some of our public facilities. It is for that reason that the chartered banks of Canada began opening on Friday night from 4.30 p.m. until 6.00 p.m. This procedure has shown itself to be a great convenience to those people who must work during banking hours. I think the larger post offices at least might consider an amendment to whatever regulation exists in relation to the hours at which wickets are open.
Then there is the regulation that covers rural routes: not more than so many, not less than so many. That may be all very well as an over-all policy or as a guide. However, I believe the application of the regulation works hardships in that it does not take account of different circumstances and of different communities. Another regulation governs the establishment of red letter boxes where people can post their mail without going all the way to the post office. Another one governs when door-to-door delivery service will be given to any special community. We have regulations in other matters. I would hope that the minister some time in the course of the next year will undertake a review of all these regulations that exist. He possibly knows how many there are. I am sure they run into the hundreds and hundreds. I hope he will make a review of them with a view of possibly eliminating half of them and instituting a little bit of common sense in the case of a goodly number of them. I know that procedure can lead to misuse as well. There is always a reason for the origin of a regulation. But I think far too often the

origin is not a very serious one and only reflects something that has gone wrong somewhere along the line.
I am a little bit alarmed, Mr. Chairman, at another phase of the minister's report for the year ended March 31, 1957. I do not know what the situation is for the year ended March 31, 1958. Maybe the minister will be able to supply that information. However, at the beginning of that post office year-I suppose that is what it would be right to call it-there were in operation 947 post offices and at the end of the year there were in operation 940 post offices or in other words a reduction in the number of post offices by seven. I may say those figures refer to the province of British Columbia. For the whole of Canada the number of post offices in operation was reduced from 11,996 to 11,879. For the whole of Canada in that one fiscal year 83 new post offices were set up and 200 post offices were closed. That means that there were 117 fewer post offices at the end of the year than at the beginning of the year. We thought the population of Canada was growing. We thought that new communities were continuously being built up in many of the unsettled areas of Canada. I should like to have an explanation. I hope the explanation is not the one that I fear it may well be. The fear to which I have reference is that there is a growing tendency to consolidate, to which even this minister has not yet called a halt, to take away from little communities their own post office in order to build up a monumental post office-and I mean monumental in size-in the larger urban centre that is nearest.
That brings me to that huge memorial that has been built in the city of Vancouver to a former minister of the government, the Vancouver post office. I admire the building. I think it is marvellous. I believe it is beautiful. All the people like to look at the building. However, I believe this post office has been established for the purpose of serving a territory much larger than the immediate area, namely the city of Vancouver. I agree that in years to come the city of Vancouver will need a post office of that size. The minister can correct me if I am wrong but I believe that the cost was some $14 million and the tunnel to the railway station added $2 million. Why in the world the government would spend money on a tunnel to a railway station from the post office when in these days most of the important mail comes in by air anyway is beyond my understanding. Interest on the $2 million would have paid for trucking charges for years and years to come without the need of the original investment. However, be

that as it may it is a nice post office and that is that.
We do not want the post offices around the city of Vancouver to have to disappear as a result of that Vancouver post office. We do not care whether the head of the post office in Vancouver is in grade 18 as a result of it and would only be in grade 9 if it were not for that centralized post office. The people want to feel that the post office belongs to them and not to a huge bureaucracy with inspectors inspecting inspectors inspecting inspectors. I know the minister is not at fault. I know this is not a policy initiated by the minister. I know that it was a previous regime that initiated that policy. However, it is not looked upon with favour by the people.
I have taken a few lessons in economics and I believe the minister has done so too. He knows that there is a point of maximum return and that if you exceed this point you no longer have efficiency but instead have inefficiency. The people in Burnaby can inform the minister that the efficiency of the postal services in their community has not improved as a result of the consolidation manoeuvres that have occurred.
I am referring to the policy of the department and am only using the lower mainland of British Columbia as an example in order to make sure that the minister knows what I am getting at. I refer to all the little services we get from the post office which usually involve 5 cents to 15 cents in respect of letters and involving 60 cents or 70 cents when we mail a parcel. They are relatively small and insignificant yet they affect the daily lives of the people who like to feel they are doing business with their own post offices.
I cannot understand why in Burnaby, where we have a population of 100,000 people, we cannot have an efficiently operated post office, when a former minister admitted that the city of Saskatoon, which has a much smaller population, has a post office which yields a net revenue to the government of Canada. So after all these years we come to the conclusion that we cannot have this post office even though we are the second largest community in our province because we have to serve the interests of that huge establishment in the city of Vancouver and if we did get our own post office some of the officials in the Vancouver post office would suffer a loss of salary or loss of category because their volume would be seriously reduced.
The post office-and this perhaps comes back to the question of regulations-might in the interest of public relations pay a little more attention to the boundaries of munici-
Supply-Post Office
palities. I know the post office has announced that it pays no attention to such boundaries and I have letters to that effect in my office. This policy leads to utter confusion and to disappointment, and it results in poor service. We have in the city of Port Moody one example, where the population within the city possibly borders on 3,000, and yet within that city is the Port Moody post office, Pleasantside post office and the city is also served from door to door by deliveries out of the city of New Westminster. Not so long ago there was an effort on the part of the post office to persuade part of the city to accept a rural route which would be based in Port Coquitlam so that there would have been four identifications in one small city. This, as I say, leads to utter confusion, and I would like the minister some day when he sends out these public notices advising the people what to do about their Christmas mail to simply take my riding as a guinea pig. I would challenge him to mail one piece of mail to every householder within my constituency without having thousands of homes not served and without having thousands of these circulars arrive in some other constituency.
There is no way of which I know, although I know the riding which I represent intimately, whereby I could send a letter to each one of my own constituents-there is no reference I could use. I have the rural directory which helps for a little bit and leads to a mix-up in some sections, and then there is the voters' list, which has no addresses at all worth mentioning. There is the telephone book and surely the Post Office Department should be able to obtain a little co-operation from the telephone companies of Canada so that at least the telephone directories might give accurate addresses. However, there is no medium of which I know available to ordinary commercial people to enable them to accurately cover any area they wish to cover. One of the major flaws is because of this regulation or decision or whatever it is that the Post Office Department will not pay attention to municipal boundaries and this has led to a case such as I have described where there are four different identifications in one little city.
There is, I believe, supposed to be a regulation in regard to the drop letter rate. I do not know what it is and I am still attempting to find out, but some small communities adjacent to communities cannot have this drop letter rate, while the riding of Coast-Capilano which was represented by a former minister and which is further away from Vancouver than some ridings does enjoy that four-cent letter rate, at least in some parts of it.

Supply-Post Office
The minister spoke to us of the financial aspects of his department and he referred to the profit making part of the mail. The first class mail, he said, is a profitable mail and I think he should give some very serious consideration to an increase in the rate for all this unnecessary material and garbage that we receive. Surely the taxpayers do not have to subsidize the Ford Motor Company or Lux soap or Rinso soap powder, or whatever else it might be, by means of taxes so that these huge corporations may be enabled not only to flood our homes with needless paper but also to overburden the backs of our mail carriers.
If the minister is thinking of instituting economies in his department and in the workload of the employees in addition to enhancing his revenues he might well recommend a realistic approach to that problem. This dates back to the very early days of Canadian history when it was in the public interest to distribute as much reading matter to the isolated pioneer as was possible, and this same principle has never been altered. Today we have the average resident in the average Canadian community receiving thousands of pounds of advertising delivered to him at the expense of a public service. This is not helping the public service at all, it is simply exploiting the taxpayer and the institutions of the taxpayer for the purposes of big business.
If one will look at the amount of money the people of Canada owe today I think it will be seen, and the minister himself must agree with this, that there has been far more advertising through the mail than there should have been for the welfare of the people during the last several years.
The points I wish to make at this stage are now fairly well covered. I think it is safe for me to say on behalf of all my colleagues that we are very pleased with the attitude taken by the minister since he took office in his department. This attitude has been one of accommodation and co-operation and we are very pleased to note the pride he takes in the honest and faithful work done by the men in this worth-while public institution and, in speaking for my own riding, I am particularly pleased to hear him say he intends to visit all post offices in Canada. I extend to him an invitation to visit the new Burnaby post office which I know he intends to have built very shortly.
Post offices in Canada are publicly owned institutions and as such they have rendered and will continue to render satisfactory services to the public only so long as and to the degree in which the people have the feeling that the individual institutions are their own. I would therefore plead with the Postmaster General to reverse the present

trend of centralization lest the institution which so many of us have grown to respect develops into an octopus which is beyond the reach of public opinion.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a minute or two to say a few words about small post offices and particularly about the salaries paid to the operators of small post offices. In my riding there are 64 small post offices and I think the top salary received by any one of these postmasters is less than $4,000. In many cases salaries range from $3,000 down. It is not possible in many of these areas where the postmaster receives such small salaries for them to have anything more than a subsistence standard of living, and unless a man can take on supplementary enterprises and step up his income by some other means he is placed in a position of having to accept a low standard of living. He gets into a position where he does not want to go out and get another job and leave his post office business because he has put in a long period of service and will qualify for a pension in the end. So he is faced with the problem of getting by as best he can and covering his costs of living out of the revenue he receives from his post office salary. As we all know, the Value of the dollar has decreased 50 per cent, and I should like to hear from the Postmaster General whether the salaries paid to these operators of small post offices have increased proportionately.
Again, I understand that the salaries are set by a rule of thumb formula which is based on the amount of work done or on the revenue of the post office. In so far as it would be possible to vary that in accordance with the conditions under which these small post office operators have to operate I think the Postmaster General would be perfectly within his right to make that variation, and I hope he does in the interest of these small operators.
In conclusion I want to add a note to what has already been said about the efficiency of the post office service. I have nothing but the greatest praise for its work in my riding. The work which is being done on the delivery routes and in these post offices is second to none. The atmosphere is good and the accommodation is good, and I think a great deal of this is attributable to the efforts of the Postmaster General.

When I called it one o'clock I indicated that there were one or two items I would like to deal with. One of them has already been introduced by the hon. member for Macleod who has just taken his seat, and I should like to follow up what he has just said. The report of the Post Office Department shows that we have 636 post offices in Newfoundland and while no breakdown is

given as to the classification of these offices I presume there is some accounting which would give the total salaries paid in Newfoundland post offices, and if the figures are available I would be grateful if the minister could give us some idea of what the average salary of the Newfoundland postmasters amount to. If he could give it for each classification, without too much inconvenience, it would be even better.
While I am talking about salaries I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that in Newfoundland and possibly everywhere else in Canada the salaries of the revenue postmasters include the amount of rent that must be paid for the post office accommodation. That was a recent change. Several years ago the post office, through the Department of Public Works, allocated the accommodation for the post office and assessed its rental and this was paid separately from the postmaster's salary. When the change was made, the postmaster was paid a fixed amount and was charged with the responsibility of finding suitable accommodation for the post office. That, of course, introduced an element of inequity, because in some places accommodation may be readily available at a reasonable price while in other communities it might not be so easily available and the cost might be higher. Unless this is taken into account the remuneration of the postmaster might be considerably reduced. Thus, in two communities with equal workloads, although the remuneration may be the same the take home pay of the individual postmasters may vary considerably on account of this policy of making the postmaster's salary cover the rental of post office accommodation.
While I am on this subject I should call the attention of the Postmaster General to the anomaly which has developed in Newfoundland due to the policy of the federal government regarding the provision of post office buildings. When the estimates for public works were before the house the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and myself tried to find out from the minister just who had the last word in determining what type of building would be supplied and the amount of space that would be provided. We learned that the local branch of the post office made an estimate of the requirements and that this was sent to the branch here in Ottawa where it would perhaps be modified or revised, and then that estimate might again be revised in consultation between the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works, but we never did find out who had the final word in determining what space should be provided. I think the minister will
Supply-Post Office
recognize that I have in mind the post office building in Marystown in my riding about which there has been a great deal of controversy and which I understand has not been started because the town council has refused to issue the necessary permit. We know that the local branch, local architects and the personnel of the Newfoundland branch estimated certain requirements for that office. That was revised by the Post Office Department here and then after further controversy it was increased, as the Minister of Public Works told us, by 20 per cent.
There is still considerable controversy over the fact that this further increase is still insufficient, having regard to the infrequency of mail. It sometimes happens that six or eight weeks mail may accumulate and arrive at the same time before it can be distributed, and those conditions obtain in most offices in Newfoundland, which makes them different from similar communities or communities of the same size on the mainland where mail can be received and distributed almost every day.
This policy with respect to buildings has caused an anomaly to develop in Newfoundland because prior to Newfoundland becoming a province of Canada the government of the island built a number of post offices in various communities where they felt the amount of traffic justified it. Those buildings were inherited by the federal government and as they become dilapidated or as they require repairs or replacement it is the policy and the responsibility of the federal government to replace them. Many of those places have now been provided with nice, up-to-date, modern post office buildings, while communities of similar size, and perhaps even greater size, and often of greater importance, cannot get a building provided by the federal department for the simple reason that it was not fortunate enough to have one prior to confederation. I would suggest to the Postmaster General that the whole policy governing the erection of post office buildings should be revised and rather than providing them on a basis of revenue, which I believe now is the case, they should be provided on merit as the requirements of the community dictate, because in a community of a thousand people, or even 500 people, it is not convenient to the public to have to go to a room in some private residence to post and receive mail. Adequate facilities for the public cannot be provided under those circumstances.
Before I leave the subject of salaries and rental of those buildings altogether I should like to ask the minister whether he can give any example where the remuneration of the postmaster has been decreased when the post

Supply-Post Office
office has been moved from a rented building, or from the residence of the postmaster, to a public building for which rent did not have to be paid? I have been told there have been such instances, and if that is so then it destroys the whole basis of the post office argument in which they maintain that they do not pay rent, they pay only the salaries of the postmasters and it is up to them to get whatever accommodation they can and pay for it out of the remuneration they receive.
Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I want to bring to the attention of the minister the position of some of our mail couriers. In Newfoundland we have very few roads and in many instances mail has to be carried either in a small boat from one settlement to another or carried overland by the courier on his back. Until quite recently I did not realize just what carrying Canadian mail is like. Before confederation we had very good regulations in Newfoundland under which the mailbag would contain bundles of letters and bundles of parcels under a certain weight, all done up in neatly wrapped packages but one courier told me this story when I discussed it with him, He said: "Sir, we are not carrying mail any more, we are carrying freight." I asked him what he meant by that. He said, "We do not carry packages, we are carrying anything, pieces of stoves, window screens and parts of washers, almost anything you can think of that can be put into a mailbag today."
These people have to carry that on their backs. I would ask the Postmaster General to take this into consideration when the remuneration of those couriers is being determined because, unlike the situation on the mainland where the courier can meet the train, deposit his mail and take mail away again, the courier in Newfoundland may have to take it to a point several miles distant. He may have to leave it there, return to his home and come back at some other time to pick up the incoming mail and carry it back to the post office. It is a much more complicated business than obtains anywhere on the mainland.
I would urge the Postmaster General to take all these factors into consideration when the remuneration of couriers is being determined.

Mr. Chairman, I was glad today to hear the Postmaster General say that we had the most efficient postal system in the world. With that I agree, but this has been so for many years. I am glad to see that the Postmaster General has followed the tradition of other postmasters general who have preceded him. This situation is due to the fact that the officials and the employees

are so loyal and so intelligent that they have helped to make our system one of the most efficient postal services in the world. I would ask the Postmaster General whether at any time he has had any intention of making any changes and whether he would consider the services that those employees have given to this country, and bear this in mind whenever he might have intentions of changing any of the personnel.
I should like to take a minute to say that when the Postmaster General was on this side of the house-and I have great regard for him and I have known him for many years- practically every day he would rise in his place in the house and denounce the once-a-day delivery. Being a businessman I approved of his action at the time. I believe he was sincere and whenever he rose to denounce the once-a-day delivery I was glad to hear him do so. And then he became a minister and, alas, he changed his mind completely. He was no longer a twice-a-day delivery fan, but he thought that the public was well served by having one delivery a day. What caused him to change his mind? He is a practical businessman. He must know that while it may not be economic as far as the post office is concerned, yet the hardship that it causes the people and the loss to the business firms in having only one delivery a day far exceeds the economies of the Post Office Department. He must realize that while it may cost the post office possibly a small amount less than it would if we had two deliveries a day yet it may be causing unemployment at a time when unemployment is rife and we need to have a job for every man. Is it really an economy? If we had these men and women working in the post office they would be drawing a salary and they would not be on the unemployment role and they would pay back in income tax possibly just as much as we are paying them now in unemployment benefits. Frankly, I do not think it is an economy. I think the minister should think back to the time when he was on the opposition side and when every day he said that we should have two deliveries a day.
The minister talked about electronic machines. I have no doubt they will be a wonderful improvement for post offices throughout the country. Automation is becoming a necessity. We must all look forward to evolution and I believe that some day we will have to have these machines. But does the minister think the time is right to introduce these machines, thus putting people out of post offices throughout the whole country because a lesser number of people will be required? I think he is making a big mistake. Possibly a few years from now

when unemployment may have ceased to exist, and I hope that it will, will be time enough to instal these machines and to put in the best systems that can be installed in our post offices throughout the country. But I think it is a very bad thing for the minister to increase the unemployment rolls at the present time. Many questions have been asked today and before I sit down I should like to ask the minister if he does not think it would be a good thing for him to reply to some of them now.

Mr. Chairman, as usual I
simply want to say a few words. My reason for rising is that I want to put before the minister a request made by the town of Acton Vale which is in another constituency than my own. Acton Vale is a progressive city and has requested me to use my influence with the Postmaster General to secure the building of a post office there. I know the city of Acton Vale very well. In recent years many industries have been established there and I think it would be most fitting if a post office would be erected there. I make this request to the Postmaster General.

Mr. Chairman, to take some point of departure in this debate, the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean was kind enough to invite me to answer some of the questions which have been asked. Well, let us take one observation he made a little while ago to which reference has also been made by a number of opposition members. I am going to use this as an example of much of what has been going on today. On May 20 of this year, as found at page 280 of Hansard, the hon. member for Outremont said:
What a wonderful difference there is between sitting in the opposition and being a member of the government.
After a few other words he went on to say:
When he was on this side of the house he protested continually about the many thefts that were taking place in the post offices throughout the country. These thefts still go on just the same and he seems to do nothing about the matter. Possibly he tries but he cannot do anything about it. If we look at all the bank robberies that are going on throughout Canada today we realize it has become almost an impossibility to check them.
All through this morning and this afternoon we have heard that same type of approach being taken in the debate. "Here is what the minister said." "Why has he not done anything about it?" All right, let us take this question as an example. The fact of the matter is that in the year ended March 31, 1958, nine months of which were under my administration, while robberies in post offices did increase from 159 in the previous
Supply-Post Office
year to 191 the actual losses in those robberies declined from $161,500 to $130,100. The reason for that is simply that instead of the previous, self-satisfied, take-what-may-come attitude of the former postmaster general we went after this thing, introduced, as I pointed out to the house this morning, various security measures and we got results and cut down losses.
More robberies.

Unfortunately we are not in a position to control the number of people who decide to break into post offices but we certainly are in a position to control the care of our own valuables. That is what we have done and it is typical of our record.
There is another point I want to make since we are on this matter. Incidentally, I want to congratulate the Liberal opposition on the excellent research they have done. Every one of them has been rustling sheets of paper containing quotations from Hansard and passing them from one to another. In fact, the finest example of this co-operation was when a couple of Liberal members rushed over to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam of the C.C.F. group when he was speaking with what they thought was a quotation which would help the hon. member. Hon. members will recall that I asked the hon. member for Vancouver East to prove what he was saying by quoting from Hansard but he could not find the quotation.
What I want to get at is this. My interest in the department and its administration has not simply arisen following my appointment as Postmaster General. A number of hon. members, and I am very grateful for it, have referred to my interest in the department and my activities over the years. Dealing specifically with the question of robberies and thefts from post offices, I have given the facts as to the results. This morning the hon. member for St. Denis asked for certain figures as to burglar alarms and thefts. I will give the figures later as to thefts but let me deal with burglar alarms for the moment because hon. members will see the development of an interesting situation.
As I said, my interest in the department has extended over a number of years. Liberal members have drawn attention to the fact that I laid great emphasis on the matter of thefts over a number of years. If we take the year 1956 we find that prior to August of that year there had only been 21 burglar alarms installed. I do not have a break-down as to how many were installed between that time and June 10, 1957, and how many after June 10, 1957, but in that period, after pressure had been exerted in this connection, 17

Supply-Post Office
more were installed or almost a 100 per cent increase in burglar alarms. There were 11 buzzer alarms before August, 1956, and that figure was increased by 50 per cent. Six were added. There had been 75 safes with money chests prior to August, 1956 and subsequent to that time another 137 were added or almost 200 per cent more.
Here is the picture of what has been happening as a result of our efforts in connection with this department. He referred specifically to Tilbury. Actually I can understand that because Tilbury is a small community with about 1,000 points of call, as we call them in the postal service, which is organizing a campaign along with some other communities right across Canada in an attempt to get thousands of signatures with which to persuade us to extend our letter carrier service down into communities of this nature.

Basically the policy which applies to letter carrier service is that it is introduced when there are 2,500 points of call in any particular community. There are other minor considerations but that is the guiding practice and the treasury board ruling is definite on that point. We have followed a policy of not extending the service until a community has reached this point and there is a specific reason for this because that is the lowest number at which it is economical to provide letter carrier service. The average letter carrier serves 500 or 600 homes; he works five days, a week and the service is provided six days a week. Therefore there must be a relief man and there must be another man to fill in on holidays and in cases of sickness and such things. It has been the experience of the department that unless there are 2,500 points of call some of these men are not fully occupied and it becomes an uneconomic proposition when you have at least half of a man sitting around-if that is possible.

The revenue post office, the smallest, is normally located in a house or in the corner of a store, and the postmaster is paid $3,000 or less, depending on the size of the business, for providing both the service and the quarters. The next type is the semi-staff post office where revenue is upwards of $3,000 and where the postmaster is under civil service regulations and where he is primarily responsible for appointing the staff underneath him. In these offices the premises are supplied by the government.

Mr. Postmaster General, we have had this equipment here since confederation". To me as a central Canadian confederation took place in 1867. I nearly fell through the floor.
