That was yet another lesson, which I have learned so many times across Canada, of just how we have different little ideas and attitudes and how we manage to get along one with another pretty well nonetheless.
With respect to the replacing of old buildings with new buildings, Mr. Chairman, which applies to Newfoundland particularly, it is specifically a matter for the Minister of Public Works. Regarding the member's request for an example, if there is one, where the remuneration of the postmaster has been decreased when he moved from his own premises to a public building, I do not have information on that point at my fingertips but I shall be glad to look it up for him and see if one exists.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works looks embarrassed.

He
just looks happy because he has such a cooperative Postmaster General who is giving him every degree of assistance that he possibly can.
On the question of mail couriers in Newfoundland, I covered that before, I think. It is by tender and if they are going to deal with these heavy packages they must adjust their tender price accordingly.
I dealt at the start with the hon. member for Outremont and some of his observations. I was interested to find that he was so vociferous and enthusiastic now in support of twice a day mail delivery. I sat in the house for four years and never heard him open his mouth on the subject and I am wondering why he did not ask for it then.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I shall refer to my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, the request of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot for a post office at Acton Vale because again that is specifically a decision of the Department of Public Works.
I apologize sincerely, Mr. Chairman, for having taken so much of the time of the committee in trying to answer the questions put to me. I have appreciated nothing quite so much as the few observations that have been made about the pride I take in the department. I do take pride in it. I think it is a very fine department, doing a very good job and for any questions that have come or will come from the floor of the house I believe we can produce pretty sensible and sound answers.

Supply-Post Office

Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the Postmaster General for his very complete and comprehensive answers and the manner in which he has answered the questions I raised. If I heard the Postmaster General correctly when he discussed the position of the people affected by the change-over by Canadian National Telegraphs he said that there were 32 revenue post offices in Newfoundland. I presume what he meant was that there are 32 revenue postmasters left over at the present time from confederation and that it is these 32 who will receive some sort of protection against the situation that has developed from the change-over by Canadian National Telegraphs.
I am most grateful to the Postmaster General for that consideration but I also suggest to him that many of the other revenue postmasters, who may have had the misfortune to become employed since confederation, are in exactly the same position as those who were employed at the time of confederation with Newfoundland. I do believe that ordinary justice demands that some consideration be given to their plight too.
With respect to the other matter I raised about the order emanating from the local post office, like the Postmaster General I find it difficult to believe that an order would go out which would be interpreted in the way in which my constituents seem to have interpreted it. But I presume that the Postmaster General will look into this and we will hear more about it later when his estimates come before the house again.

That is right, although I had hoped that we might get these estimates through today. If that should happen, I certainly will give the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo complete information without any hesitation.

I will not delay the minister's estimates another minute. The only other point I wish to make has to do with what he had to say about couriers. He said that they received the amount that they offered to accept when they tendered. I should like to point out to the Postmaster General that these mail couriers are at a disadvantage when submitting tenders because they do not really understand what they are tendering for. They visualize an ordinary bag of mail made up of bundles of letters and a few nicely wrapped packages. But they discover later than instead of carrying little packets of letters and a few packages they are carrying heavy objects and articles like doors, windows, screens, parts of washing machines and garden implements and other things which they do not regard as mail. If they had known that this was what they were
(Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace).]
tendering for I think they would have submitted quite different tenders. In view of the disadvantage at which they find themselves I still think they have a case when they ask that their tenders be revised.

Mr. Chairman, during the last half hour the minister has made quite an attempt to explain away statements he made in years gone by dealing with a twice a day delivery system. I feel that many of us here now who were here at that time will not readily forget the manner in which he proposed twice a day mail delivery and the frequency with which he made mention of it. During his remarks he rather left the impression that when he first came to the house this particular problem was of current interest and that over a period of four or five years public interest began to diminish and there was no longer the same need to express his opinion on the problem as there had been before.
I remember quite well when the hon. member made his maiden speech in the first session of the twenty-second parliament. At that time he gave quite an account of the need for a twice a day mail delivery system in the area from which he comes. I am going to read from the speech he made then. At that time he said, as recorded on page 343 of Hansard for the 1953-54 session:
Our postal service is totally inadequate for the needs of a community such as ours. While we are essentially a residential community, stores and businesses are scattered throughout the area. We have numerous salesmen and representatives who combine both home and office. For some reason which was defended on the grounds of economy, but which still did not seem to result in any great reduction in the Post Office Department expenses mail delivery in our area was reduced a few years ago from twice a day to once a day. This has caused us a great deal of inconvenience. My riding is an integral part of a great city. It is a busy place with many interests, and it is dependent upon an adequate postal service. Many of these activities are being seriously handicapped and inconvenienced by a postal service which would be more appropriate for a small, sleepy country village.
Then he went on to say:
We feel that we are entitled to the restoration of adequate postal facilities.
I would say to him, having said that, that surely the need for postal service in the area from which he comes has not decreased from that time to now. I am quite sure that it has not. If this country is going to expand at the rate we are told by some of the hon. gentleman's colleagues then we can look forward to the time when necessarily the larger and busier centres will be still larger and busier. I suspect that in that sense they will require a more adequate

postal service. I say to the minister now that if such a service was required in 1953-54 it is still required.
In his remarks the minister went on to say that since then there has been no great public demand for this service. Yet only a year ago he himself still maintained the same opinion. I quote again from page 1807 of Hansard for March 1, 1957. The hon. member for Levis has already referred to this but I am going to read the whole paragraph. Just over a year ago when he was sitting on this side of the house the minister said:
Let me say immediately that there is no quarrel with the rural areas in their demand for a minimum delivery once a day, nor is there any doubt in the mind of any of us, I think, that certain areas now on rural routes or on box systems are entitled to twice a day delivery. The point I would make is that the elimination of twice a day mail delivery service has caused and is continuing to cause considerable distress and inconvenience in our metropolitan areas that are now served by letter carrier service. The costs were worked out in detail and presented to the estimates committee last year They represented approximately one-third of the surplus of the post office department for the year 1955-56, and they will represent less than one-half of the estimated surplus of the post office department for the current year. In other words, we could change to twice a day delivery service, five days a week, and still leave the post office department with a substantial surplus.
These are the words of the minister just over a year ago. Well, I fail to see how the minister is going to square his statement of a year ago with the statement he makes now that it is going to be too expensive. I suggest the metamorphosis of changing from an ordinary member of this house to a minister by crossing 20 feet of green carpet to sit on the treasury benches, is one that changed him from making irresponsible statements to being faced with the realities of life. I am glad that he has done that. I hope that in facing these realities of life in the Post Office Department, he will face a few of the realities in the province from which I come. I am going to tell him about those.
In a section of Newfoundland which is thickly populated for that province, the mail service is most unsatisfactory. The fault is not all that of the Post Office Department, but a great deal of it is the result of the fact that mail deliveries by the Canadian National or other boats, or in the wintertime by airplane, are not too regular. I am not going to blame the minister or his department for that. I do feel that after the mail has been landed in that area some better method could be found for delivery from the point of landing to the various places along the coast. I have made some inquiries about this problem, but to date I have not made much progress.
I go farther up along the west coast of Newfoundland, along what is known as the
Supply-Post Office
St. Barbe coast and I come to a place known as Hawke's Bay, which is a large logging centre. The resident population may number 600 or 700 people, but during the logging season which lasts over a period of some months, the population will increase sometimes by 2,000 people. These 2,000 people come from all sections of the coast. They do not live in Hawke's Bay, and being away from home they are naturally looking for mail. The mail service to this particular place is most unsatisfactory because the place is a little isolated. During the coming summer Hawke's Bay will be connected with one of the largest centres known as Port Saunders by a road which is now being built by the provincial government. I should like to recommend to the minister that when that road is completed the mail service could be improved at a more reasonable cost than it could have been improved last year. I suggest serious attention be given to improving the mail service for Hawke's Bay.
Then I made a request of the minister about a place called Portland Creek. In explaining about Portland Creek I would have to explain the situation that obtains within this section of Newfoundland because the mail is now able to come from an area known as Norris Point down the coast by road, but that has only been possible within the last year. So, when the mail goes from Cow Head down to Daniel's Harbour the mail carrier has actually to pass through Portland Creek. Although Portland Creek is five miles away from the nearest post office I have so far been unable to obtain any mail service for this particular place. I would hope that when the minister's estimates are through and he has time to look over things that are going to be done in the future, he will take into account this little isolated settlement of Portland Creek.
I come now, Mr. Chairman, to the question of the post office at a very lovely settlement called St. Andrews on the west coast of Newfoundland. The minister is well aware now of the conditions under which Newfoundland came into confederation so far as the postal service is concerned, and is well aware of the conditions under which some buildings were taken over as federal buildings while other buildings remained in the provincial service. Here is a building which is now federal, which is very old and no longer able to meet the needs of that area. I am not so much concerned, Mr. Chairman, with whether the building itself be large or small, so long as it is adequate. I think the building which is known as the post office should be something of a credit to the federal government. It should be a

Supply-Post Office
decent looking building. I think the Postmaster General would want that type of building. I can assure him that this little building is no longer adequate to meet the needs of the people whom it serves; it is in a most dilapidated condition. I fear that some day when there is a good Newfoundland breeze this building will not stand on all fours as it has in the past. I do hope that something can be done about this to avoid any accident that might happen, and also to improve the service in that area.
In my correspondence with the department concerning this place, I fear that there has been some misunderstanding and they think I am speaking about some other place. In one letter I had from the department it was stated that this place received postal service in the summertime only. Of course, this is not true because it is served by two trains every day and is served by road during all seasons of the year and even in wintertime this road is accessible. It is quite often the centre to which mail is brought and from which mail is delivered to various points around it. I hope that it may be possible for the minister to have a look at this building and to decide that the service which it provides is not suitable for the Post Office Department. Then we could make a recommendation to my good friend the Minister of Public Works, who may be able to do something about this particular problem. I am sure the construction would not be costly and could be completed within a short time.
Jutting out from the west coast of Newfoundland is an area of land known as the Port au Port peninsula. This Port au Port peninsula has only one main point of contact with the mainland, which has a large and thriving town of Stephenville, on the borders of which the United States has had for some years a very large air force base. I am not going to give the minister a description of the mail service on Port au Port peninsula. I am going to suggest to him a survey be made of the needs of the area all along that Port au Port peninsula to ascertain what can be done to improve the service for the people who live there. Not too long ago, when the people who live within the Port au Port peninsula found work at the air force base in Stephenville, they were able to collect their mail at the local post office at Stephenville. Times are changing there and more people, by reason of having to be employed somehow, are returning to the fishing industry and are living continuously in the areas in which their homes are built. These people are feeling more keenly as time goes on the

need for postal service which will be an improvement over the service now provided.
I do not want to delay the minister too long, but we have in Newfoundland numerous small buildings that are serving as post offices. Sometimes the post offices are separate buildings, sometimes they are in rooms in private houses or in a section of a store, something of that type. In many of these cases we find that the rent being paid by the postal department would not pay for the charwoman to clean up after the mail has been delivered. I recommend to the minister that a very serious attempt be made to see what can be done about renting these buildings. I will agree that many of the people who are getting little or no rent at the moment are a little bit afraid to say too much about it because they fear that the community would lose the postal service as there would be no place to house the post office. In many of these cases, the rent being paid is very small. It is really too small, as I said before, to pay for the coal and the cleaning up. It is far too small to warrant anybody building a building, even a building which might be rented in the area. I would ask the hon. gentleman if he would, if time permits, go into this whole problem of building rentals for the post office services in Newfoundland.
I intended to have something to say about the Canadian National Telegraphs and its connection with the postal service. However, my hon. friend for Burin-Burgeo has gone into that matter. I believe it is a most gnawing problem and one that is not conducive to the best of efficiency either in the post office or in the Canadian National Telegraphs. However, I am going to reserve my comments in this regard and possibly make them at a later date when the estimates of the Minister of Transport are before the house.

As we all now know, Mr. Chairman, co-operation exists between the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works. While they are both here and having regard to the construction of post office buildings, maybe one of the two or the two together could give me this information. Can the minister tell the committee when tenders will be called for the construction of a new postal station in the city of Cote St. Luc in the constituency of Mount Royal? Have plans been drawn? Who is the architect? When is the construction likely to start? I believe the minister in answer to the hon. member for Mount Royal stated that the building of the post office has been decided on.

Yes. In that particular case it has been decided to put up this building. The plans are now

being drawn. Tenders will be called, I would think,-according to the information which I have received-in order to allow construction to start about mid-October of this year.

I want to ask the minister what policy he follows in the recommendation of the construction of new post offices. Does he make a recommendation only in cases where the revenue of the post office is $10,000 or does he do so when it is less than that?

There is a certain amount of elasticity. Certainly it is not our practice to recommend construction of post offices in areas where the revenue is less than $10,000. Where the revenue goes over that amount we may sometimes recommend the construction of a post office and find that the Department of Public Works can provide more than adequate rental space which in their judgment is better. In other cases-and there are not very many of these-where the revenue is less than $10,000 the Department of Public Works may be planning a building to incorporate two or three units in the community and decide to include us in that building. Generally, the breaking point at which one moves into the construction of a public building for a post office is $10,000.

I should like to ask the
minister whether construction of a postal station is planned for Rosemount. I remember that at the end of 1957 we exchanged correspondence with the previous postmaster general. Since Rosemount is a district which is developing very rapidly it is felt that a new station is in order in that district. Can the minister tell me whether there is anything on the way?

speechtext:
I am
sorry to keep the hon. gentleman waiting. I will have the information in just a moment.
Perhaps I can help the minister out by stating that the site was on Pie IX boulevard near the new shopping centre.

speechtext:

information I have at the moment is that there is nothing immediately on the way in connection with Rosemount.
I wonder whether the minister can tell us what has been done this year with regard to housing for post office employees in the Northwest Territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
That is a problem which does not apply particularly to the Post Office Department but which is generally a matter of government policy. I believe it is under study; that
Supply-Post Office
is to say, the provision of quarters for government employees in the north is under study by a committee of the government. As the hon. member will notice, there is a substantial increase in the amount of our estimates for the provision of this accommodation owing to the fact that we are obliged to pay more for certain forms of taxation and provision of services in the north.

A year or so ago it was government policy that the Post Office Department supply housing at least for two of their employees, namely the postmaster in Fort Smith and the postmaster in Yellowknife. These buildings were to be completed last year. My question now relates to housing for the employees of the Post Office Department other than the postmaster himself. In this particular case, I imagine that Yellowknife would be about the only place where employees would have to be supplied with houses in order to bring their standards in line with those of employees of other government departments.
wish I could give the hon. member the details that he requires now; but actually, as I understand it, this is purely an extension of the housing of government employees in the north.
Is anything being done this year?

To
the best of my knowledge, the matter is still under study by a committee of the government.
Then nothing has been done this year to provide any additional housing units in the Northwest Territories?
That is right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Le Droit of September 25, 1957, carries a report of a speech made by the minister before the advertising and sales club of Ottawa which is an organization dear to the heart of the minister, I know. The statement which he is reported to have made had to do with publicity as a means of communication between the government and the public. Perhaps he had in mind the post office at the time; I do not know whether or not that is so, Then he went on to say that in the last budget presented to parliament-that is not the one that was under discussion recently- expenditures of all departments amounted to slightly over $4J billion which means the expenditure of about a dollar on publicity for each $900 spent on other matters. The

Supply-Post Office
question I should like to ask the minister now is whether he has been able to increase that amount set out in the speech referred to in Le Droit, I think an example was given by the minister at that time. The reason I raise the point is that I understand that this matter has been under consideration by the departmental officials. I wondered whether the minister had anything to say on that matter.

On
the broader picture which affected the total government expenditures and total government disbursements in respect of advertising and publicity, I know the hon. member would agree with me that it would be quite improper for me to make any wide-ranging observations which are more properly the responsibility of the Prime Minister.
As far as our own department is concerned, at this moment our expenditures-and I can give them to the hon. member exactly-are very much in line with those of the preceding year, subject however to a reduction due to the fact that our film was paid for largely in the preceding year. We are now contemplating certain aspects of future operations which may require public co-operation with respect to such things as the zoning of mail if that should become once more an active issue such as in a case where a person in addition to putting the city on the address will also put a particular location within that city.
This might require additional expenditures because the purpose of expenditures on publicity and advertising is to achieve some result which will merit such expenditures, and I can assure the hon. member that any expenditures we make will be in order to achieve a specific result.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I press the minister a little further with regard to this matter. Is there an increase over the amount for last year of this kind of advertising?

The
figure which was in the estimates for 1957-58 was $255,300, covering expenditures on advertising, films, broadcasting and displays, while the figure for the current year is $216,700. That is a decrease of $38,600. The decrease is primarily, as I have said, due to the fact that the post office film was paid for in the preceding year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a further question. According to the Ottawa Journal of September 10, 1957, the minister made a statement referring to the 12,000 rural mail carriers in Canada, and I quote his words which were reported as follows:
12,000 rural mail carriers in Canada have been warned to refrain from political activities at the

risk of losing their contracts with the dominion government. A Post Office Department directive to be read by all mail contractors was approved by Postmaster General Hamilton a month ago and has gone forward to post office districts over the signature of Sarto Chartrand, post office director of transportation.
May I ask the minister if following this statement and because of the directive referred to there have been any dismissals from the post office?

In
the case of rural mail carriers, Mr. Chairman, the answer is no. The hon. member is asking now about political activity on the part of rural mail carriers?

The
answer is no.

Some weeks ago I noticed in the Edmonton Journal that the Post Office Department was now routing mail for Uranium City, Saskatchewan, via Saskatoon and Prince Albert rather than, as formerly, via Edmonton by C.P.A. to Uranium City. I wonder if the minister could give us the reason why this service has been changed and could also give us an idea of the cost of transporting mail from Saskatoon to Uranium City as against Edmonton to Uranium City?

will be delighted to give the hon. member the information he requires. Actually it is a technical matter having to do with our transportation vote and if he would wait for a moment or two until the expert on this question is here and we come to that item in the estimates I will be glad to give him an answer.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I pursue the question I asked concerning political patronage a little further? The minister has said that no rural mail carriers have been dismissed and I would like to ask whether in any other branches of the post office there have been dismissals because of political patronage?

Mr. Chairman, there has not been a single dismissal in my department because of political patronage in the way suggested by the hon. member. However, I think I know what he is trying to get at and I want to help him if I can. There has been one dismissal for political activity on the part of an employee in respect of which an affidavit is on file from the employee concerned admitting the particular political activity.
A few minutes ago the minister told us that the international postal convention held in Ottawa last year cost $225,000.
What I said was $226,000.
$226,000-would he give us the breakdown as to hospitality, transportation, staff, and so on?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, this is something we have available because we felt sure someone would be interested in it. I do not know how much detail the hon. member would like but I will give him a reasonable amount and if he finds it insufficient I will give him more.
The administration covering salaries of House of Commons staff was $22,000-I will give these in round figures-the reporters' travelling and living expenses were $3,000; the travelling and living expenses of certain other non-Canadian people were $4,500; expenses of printing, stationery and various other items totalled $55,900; sundries in that classification were $460; provision of equipment for simultaneous translation and so on, $6,790; provision of accommodation-and I here refer to accommodation when we were travelling and when these people were our guests in various parts of Canada, and the same applies to the following two or three items-$33,384; meals under the same circumstances, $20,850; entertaining in Ottawa and elsewhere of specific people, $3,090; gifts, because it is customary at these international conventions to present them with a booklet of stamps of the country concerned and to provide other publicity items which are given as souvenirs of the country-$15,000; transportation in connection with trips, $21,800; and the delegates were also given very adequate photographic albums and coverage costing $4,160, and that adds up roughly to $192,000, to which we add $34,000 from the previous year's expenditures, mostly in connection with the system of simultaneous translation, for a grand total of $226,000.
May I ask the minister if he has disposed of that system of simultaneous translation?

As
I remember it, Mr. Chairman, this never belonged to us; it was equipment which was the property of the national defence department. Could the minister tell us the number of people employed in administration in the province of Newfoundland and the cost of administration in that province and could he also give us the same information with respect to the province of Nova Scotia?

I am
sorry, but I have not that information available. I will be very glad to give it to the hon. member during the debate, or see that it is sent to him.

Talking about expenses, may I ask the minister about the item under travelling expenses amounting to $80,000 on page 438. And then if the minister will turn to page 442 he will see there under travelling expenses an amount of $387,750. I have here a statement which was made by the hon. gentleman while he was in opposition, and I quote from his remarks at page 4186 of Hansard on May 27, 1955:
Finally ... I would ask the minister to tell us why his travelling expenses have had to go up from $35,300 to $100,400. Even with all the effort put forward by this government in finding new and fanciful ways of spending public money, that is an accomplishment of which he may well be proud.
Of course, the hon. minister was then talking about the expenses of the department and not about the expenses of the Postmaster General himself. Now I have just mentioned a couple of items amounting to at least $460,000, and I ask the minister whether he is in a position to explain this large increase in travelling expenses and, if he is not in a position to do this, whether he will apply to himself the remarks he made about the former minister?

course, the increase in travelling expenses in this particular estimate has not been anything like as great as the increase to which the hon. member has just referred in the estimates of the previous minister. I think it was from $35,000-

To $100,400.

Supply-Post Office

In
other words, when you find an increase of from $35,000 to $100,000, that is quite legitimately the cause of a question. The particular case we are discussing concerns $80,000 in the estimates as against $80,000-the same amount-in the estimates for the preceding year, and in the other case it is $387,750 as against $345,150, an increase which is slightly over 10 per cent. The reason, of course, for our travelling expenses is that we have a fantastically far-flung postal department with headquarters in Ottawa and the necessity of covering all Canada to inspect post offices, and to have officials dealing with special situations. Mr. Chairman, is this the estimate where we can ask the minister what the additional cost would be to have a twice a day delivery?

will be glad to give that figure. It is $80,000 under administration, $387,750 under operations, $10,000 under transportation and $3,500 under financial services. That is $479,000 I think.

subtopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT INQUIRIES
COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT INQUIRIES
speechtext:
1.	How many inquiries under the Combines Investigation Act were instituted during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958?
2.	How many of these were made (a) under section 7 of the act; (b) ordered by the director; (c) by order of the minister?
3.	In each case, what was the nature of the alleged offence and the names and addresses of the persons, organizations or corporations involved?
4.	Which of such inquiries (a) are still under investigation; (b) were discontinued; (c) referred to the restrictive trade practices commission; (d) resulted in prosecution or other legal proceedings being taken?
Answer by: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of
Justice):
1.	Sixteen.
2.	(a) None; (b) fifteen such inquiries were commenced by the director pursuant to section 8(b) of the Combines Investigation Act which provides that the director shall cause an inquiry to be made whenever he has reason to believe that the sections of the anti-combines legislation have been, are being or are about to be violated. One such inquiry was commenced by the director pursuant to section 42 of the act which provides that the director may carry out an inquiry concerning the existence and effect of conditions or practices relating to any commodity which may be the subject of trade or commerce and which conditions or practices are related to monopolistic practices or restraint of trade; (c) none.
3.	Five of the inquiries relate to the merger, trust or monopoly provision (section 2(e)); four relate to combinations in restraint of trade; five relate to predatory or discriminatory pricing (section 412 of the Criminal
Questions
Code); one relates to resale price maintenance; and one relates to section 42 of the Combines Investigation Act above mentioned. It is not considered advisable or appropriate to publish further details relating to an inquiry unless and until a report has been made to and published by the minister.
4.(a) Fifteen; (b) one; (c) one; (d) none.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION ON NARCOTIC CONTROL
INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION ON NARCOTIC CONTROL
speechtext:
1.	Has the government received from or through the United Nations a copy of the proposed convention to replace all existing international treaties for the international control of narcotics?
2.	If so, was the Canadian government asked for comments on this proposed convention?
3.	What reply has been made by the government?
Answer by: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary
of State for External Affairs):
The draft single convention on narcotic drugs underwent some revision at the thirteenth session of the narcotics commission of the economic and social council which met in Geneva in May this year. The commission agreed that the text of the convention as revised should be forwarded to the economic and social council with a recommendation that it be referred to governments by the secretary general for comment and that a plenipotentiary conference be convened in 1960 for consideration of it.
The economic and social council is meeting at present in Geneva. If it approves the recommendations of the narcotics commission we can expect that the convention will be sent to governments for their comments shortly after the session which is due to end on August 2, 1958.
